We contribute two audit-targeted repair operations: preference-rank selection raises judge accuracy on paired responses from $65.0\%$ to $68.6\%$, competitive with the strongest rubric-discovery baselines and leading on two of three judges in our cross-judge sweep; reliability-constrained refinement reduces the rate at which exploit responses receive high scores from $46.4\%$ to $36.0\%$ with little change in inter-judge agreement ($α{=}.531\to.519$).

AI.tldr: PReMISE is a framework that discovers and audits rubrics for LLM judges, showing that no single rubric source is simultaneously reliable, preference-predictive, and adversarially robust, while introducing repair operations that improve judge accuracy from 65.0% to 68.6% and reduce exploitability from 46.4% to 36.0%.
AI.motivation: LLM judges' evaluations of open-ended responses are highly sensitive to the rubrics they are conditioned on; vague rubrics (e.g., "helpful and factual") can reward polished but factually incorrect or intent-violating answers, motivating the need for systematic rubric design and auditing.
AI.method: PReMISE framework: (i) discovers a policy-level rubric set from pairwise human-preference data, and (ii) audits any rubric set along four axes: structural adequacy, reliability, preference fit, and adversarial robustness. Two repair operations: preference-rank selection and reliability-constrained refinement.
AI.result: No raw rubric source is simultaneously reliable, preference-predictive, and adversarially robust. High inter-rater agreement does not imply low exploitability. PReMISE is the only rubric source scoring non-trivially on applicability, specificity, and effective dimensionality. Preference-rank selection raises accuracy from 65.0% to 68.6%. Reliability-constrained refinement reduces exploit response high-score rate from 46.4% to 36.0% with minimal change in inter-judge agreement (α=.531→.519).
AI.conclusion: Rubric design is a measurement specification problem; systematic auditing and targeted repair operations can substantially improve LLM judge performance, with PReMISE uniquely balancing multiple quality axes simultaneously.

title: Object-Informed Model Predictive Path Integral Control for Non-Prehensile Robot Manipulation
summary: Long-horizon planning for non-prehensile robot manipulation is challenging due to underactuated and discontinuous interactions. We propose a hierarchical formulation of model predictive path integral (MPPI) control that guides robot-level planning with a separately computed object-level plan to achieve efficient long-horizon prediction. We first solve a simplified object-only problem, assuming the object can be actuated directly, and use the planned object trajectory as a reference in solving the joint robot-object planning problem. We evaluate our method in both simulation and hardware using a 6-DoF xArm6 manipulator to perform object pushing tasks in which the target object must reach a goal while avoiding static obstacles, necessitating non-myopic reasoning. Our object-informed MPPI increases task success by 40\% with a 26\% faster control frequency in simulation, and by 20\% in real experiments with similar computation as regular MPPI.

AI.tldr: A hierarchical MPPI control framework uses a simplified object-level plan to guide robot-level planning, improving long-horizon non-prehensile manipulation by 40% in simulation and 20% in real experiments with faster control frequency.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon planning for non-prehensile robot manipulation is challenging due to underactuated and discontinuous interactions, requiring non-myopic reasoning to handle tasks like pushing objects to goals while avoiding obstacles.
AI.method: A hierarchical formulation of MPPI control that first solves a simplified object-only problem (assuming direct object actuation) and uses the planned object trajectory as a reference to guide the joint robot-object planning problem.
AI.result: 40% higher task success and 26% faster control frequency in simulation; 20% higher task success in real experiments with similar computation as regular MPPI using a 6-DoF xArm6 manipulator.
AI.conclusion: Object-informed hierarchical MPPI enables efficient long-horizon prediction and non-myopic reasoning for non-prehensile manipulation tasks with static obstacles, outperforming regular MPPI.

title: Planner-Centric Reinforcement Learning for Deep Research with Structure-Aware Reward
summary: Deep research tasks require LLMs to plan what to investigate, retrieve evidence, and synthesize long-form answers across multiple branches of inquiry. Existing training paradigms either rely on short-form verifiable QA as a proxy or optimize monolithic long trajectories, which makes planning and execution difficult to disentangle and yields weak credit assignment for the planning process. We propose DecomposeR, a planner-centric deep research framework that represents research plans as typed directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), allowing planning to be made explicit, structured, and rewardable. We train a Qwen3-8B model in two stages: planner reinforcement learning (RL) first learns graph structure and query decomposition to improve research planning, and answerer reinforcement learning (RL) then learns branch-level execution and final synthesis conditioned on the learned plan. By assigning rewards to explicit planner tokens and structured components rather than to a flat trajectory, DecomposeR enables finer-grained optimization of planning while reducing the ambiguity of end-to-end training. Experiments show that DecomposeR-8B improves over strong comparable open baselines by 5.1-8.0 points on popular long-form benchmarks due to improved planning and answering capabilities.

AI.tldr: DecomposeR is a planner-centric deep research framework that represents research plans as typed DAGs, trains a Qwen3-8B model via two-stage reinforcement learning (planner RL + answerer RL), and achieves 5.1-8.0 point improvements on long-form benchmarks over comparable open baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing training paradigms for deep research tasks either rely on short-form verifiable QA as a proxy or optimize monolithic long trajectories, making planning and execution difficult to disentangle and yielding weak credit assignment for the planning process.
AI.method: Proposes DecomposeR, which represents research plans as typed directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) and trains a Qwen3-8B model in two stages: planner RL learns graph structure and query decomposition, then answerer RL learns branch-level execution and final synthesis conditioned on the learned plan. Rewards are assigned to explicit planner tokens and structured components rather than flat trajectories.
AI.result: DecomposeR-8B improves over strong comparable open baselines by 5.1-8.0 points on popular long-form benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: By enabling finer-grained optimization of planning through explicit structured rewards, DecomposeR reduces the ambiguity of end-to-end training and improves both planning and answering capabilities for deep research tasks.

title: Two Degree-of-Freedom Vibratory Transport in a Grasp
summary: In this paper, we use asymmetric vibrations to demonstrate two degree-of-freedom (DoF) in-hand manipulation of grasped parts. The asymmetric vibrations are achieved through closed-loop position control of a moving surface, which applies a periodic stick-slip waveform to the part to be manipulated. We show analytically how two vibratory waveform parameters, the sticking acceleration and the slipping acceleration, affect average part velocity when moving against gravity. The theoretical trends are then validated using an experimental setup where the squeeze force is controlled and part motion is recorded by a high-resolution encoder. We also develop a 2-DoF vibratory surface capable of translation in one direction and rotation about the surface normal. Using two of these 2-DoF surfaces in a parallel jaw gripper configuration, we bidirectionally translate and rotate a variety of grasped parts, as well as demonstrate that the same waveform trends for translation also persist for in-plane rotation.

AI.tldr: This paper uses asymmetric vibrations (periodic stick-slip waveforms) via closed-loop position control to achieve 2-DoF in-hand manipulation (translation and rotation) of grasped parts. The effects of sticking and slipping acceleration on part velocity are analyzed theoretically and validated experimentally. A 2-DoF vibratory surface (translation + rotation) is used in a parallel jaw gripper to bidirectionally manipulate various parts.
AI.motivation: To enable two degree-of-freedom in-hand manipulation of grasped parts using asymmetric vibrations, providing a method for precise part positioning without complex mechanisms.
AI.method: Asymmetric vibrations generated by closed-loop position control of a moving surface with a periodic stick-slip waveform. Theoretical analysis of how sticking acceleration and slipping acceleration affect average part velocity against gravity. Experimental validation with controlled squeeze force and high-resolution encoder recording. A 2-DoF vibratory surface enabling translation and rotation was developed and used in a parallel jaw gripper configuration.
AI.result: Theoretical trends for sticking and slipping acceleration effects on part velocity were validated experimentally. The 2-DoF vibratory surfaces in a parallel jaw gripper successfully bidirectionally translated and rotated various grasped parts. The same waveform trends for translation were shown to persist for in-plane rotation.
AI.conclusion: Asymmetric vibrations with controlled stick-slip waveforms can effectively achieve 2-DoF in-hand manipulation (translation and rotation) of grasped parts, and the waveform parameter trends generalize from translational to rotational manipulation.

title: SLAT: Segment-Level Adaptive Trimming for Efficient CoT Reasoning
summary: Recent advances in Large Reasoning Models have significantly improved chain-of-thought (CoT) capabilities via reinforcement learning (RL). However, generated reasoning chains frequently suffer from structural redundancy (i.e., \emph{overthinking}), incurring high computational overhead without improving answer correctness. Existing mitigation strategies typically rely on token-uniform length penalties, which provide coarse, segment-agnostic pressure toward shorter outputs and can inadvertently suppress useful reasoning alongside redundancy. To address this, we demonstrate that inefficiency concentrates in high-probability segments with low marginal utility. We derive a theoretical characterization of segment suboptimality under the correctness-length trade-off objective and propose \textsc{SLAT} (Segment-Level Adaptive Trimming), an RL framework that selectively suppresses redundant segments based on this criterion. Empirical results on standard benchmarks indicate that \textsc{SLAT} establishes a superior accuracy-efficiency Pareto frontier, reducing reasoning length by $50\%$ relative to uncompressed baselines while maintaining competitive accuracy. Overall, our results suggest that theoretically grounded, segment-aware trimming is a promising direction for efficient CoT reasoning in large language models.

AI.tldr: SLAT is a segment-level RL framework that reduces chain-of-thought reasoning length by ~50% while maintaining accuracy, by selectively trimming high-probability, low-utility segments.
AI.motivation: Current RL-trained Large Reasoning Models produce chain-of-thought reasoning with structural redundancy (overthinking), causing high computational cost without accuracy gain. Existing length penalties are token-uniform and segment-agnostic, failing to distinguish useful reasoning from redundancy.
AI.method: The authors derive a theoretical characterization of segment suboptimality under the correctness-length trade-off, then propose SLAT (Segment-Level Adaptive Trimming), an RL framework that selectively suppresses redundant segments based on low marginal utility in high-probability regions.
AI.result: SLAT establishes a superior accuracy-efficiency Pareto frontier, reducing reasoning length by ~50% versus uncompressed baselines while maintaining competitive accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Theoretically grounded, segment-aware trimming is a promising direction for efficient CoT reasoning in large language models.

title: Feat2Go: Visual Feature-Grounded Value Estimation for Embodied Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reinforcement learning is a promising approach for improving the capabilities of vision-language-action (VLA) models while avoiding the heavy data requirements of imitation learning. However, its effectiveness for VLA models is often constrained by sparse supervision and the difficulty of designing informative reward signals for long-horizon manipulation. In this work, we present Feat2Go, a fine-grained value estimation framework for embodied reinforcement learning. Specifically, Feat2Go first derives a continuous progress target from a pretrained visual world model by measuring patch-level similarity to subgoal states and partitioning episodes into semantic stages with trend-based clustering. We then train an embodied value model to predict this structural progress from the current observation and task instruction, and use the predicted value to reshape terminal rewards during policy optimization. The proposed framework is compatible with existing VLA policy reinforcement learning pipelines, including PPO and GRPO, and does not rely on manual reward engineering. Extensive experiments on ManiSkill3 and RoboTwin 2.0 demonstrate that Feat2Go consistently improves the performance of existing VLA models under both single-arm and bimanual manipulation settings. More specifically, on ManiSkill3, Feat2Go improves OpenVLAOFT from 17.5% to 82.9% average out-of-distribution success while retaining 96.9% in-distribution performance. On RoboTwin 2.0, Feat2Go achieves an average success rate of 88.8% in domain-randomized task settings, outperforming prior reinforcement learning methods.

AI.tldr: Feat2Go is a fine-grained value estimation framework that uses a pretrained visual world model to derive continuous progress targets via patch-level similarity and trend-based clustering, then trains an embodied value model to predict this progress for reward reshaping in VLA policy RL, achieving significant improvements on ManiSkill3 (82.9% OOD success, 96.9% ID retention) and RoboTwin 2.0 (88.8% average success).
AI.motivation: Reinforcement learning for VLA models is often constrained by sparse supervision and difficulty of designing informative reward signals for long-horizon manipulation tasks.
AI.method: Feat2Go first derives a continuous progress target from a pretrained visual world model by measuring patch-level similarity to subgoal states and partitioning episodes into semantic stages via trend-based clustering. It then trains an embodied value model to predict this structural progress from current observation and task instruction, using the predicted value to reshape terminal rewards during policy optimization. Compatible with PPO and GRPO, no manual reward engineering.
AI.result: On ManiSkill3, Feat2Go improves OpenVLA-OFT from 17.5% to 82.9% average OOD success while retaining 96.9% in-distribution performance. On RoboTwin 2.0, achieves 88.8% average success rate in domain-randomized settings, outperforming prior RL methods.
AI.conclusion: Feat2Go consistently improves VLA model performance under both single-arm and bimanual manipulation settings without manual reward engineering, demonstrating a practical framework for fine-grained value estimation in embodied RL.

title: COMPASS: Cognitive MCTS-Guided Process Alignment for Safe Search Agents
summary: LLM-powered search agents enable multi-step reasoning and tool use. However, these capabilities introduce retrieval-induced safety degradation, as harmful intents may decompose into seemingly innocuous sub-queries that lead to unsafe outcomes. Existing alignment methods struggle to capture sparse safety signals and fail to supervise diverse violations across multi-step interactions. We propose COMPASS, a Cognitive MCTS-Guided Process Alignment framework designed to achieve robust safety alignment throughout the agent workflow while preserving general utility. COMPASS integrates cognitive tree exploration (CTE) to efficiently synthesize stealthy attack trajectories, and introspective step-wise alignment (ISA) to isolate risky intermediate actions for fine-grained process supervision. Empirical results show that COMPASS achieves a favorable safety-utility trade-off while requiring substantially less training data.

AI.tldr: COMPASS is a safety alignment framework for LLM-powered search agents that uses cognitive MCTS-guided process alignment to detect and mitigate retrieval-induced safety degradation from decomposed harmful queries, achieving strong safety-utility trade-offs with less training data.
AI.motivation: LLM-powered search agents with multi-step reasoning and tool use suffer from retrieval-induced safety degradation, where harmful intents decompose into seemingly innocuous sub-queries that lead to unsafe outcomes. Existing alignment methods struggle to capture sparse safety signals and fail to supervise diverse violations across multi-step interactions.
AI.method: COMPASS integrates two key components: (1) Cognitive Tree Exploration (CTE) to efficiently synthesize stealthy attack trajectories, and (2) Introspective Step-wise Alignment (ISA) to isolate risky intermediate actions for fine-grained process supervision.
AI.result: COMPASS achieves a favorable safety-utility trade-off while requiring substantially less training data compared to existing alignment methods.
AI.conclusion: The proposed cognitive MCTS-guided process alignment framework effectively achieves robust safety alignment throughout the agent workflow while preserving general utility, addressing the unique safety challenges posed by multi-step LLM agents.

title: Hide-and-Seek in Trajectories: Discovering Failure Signals for VLA Runtime Monitoring
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models enable robots to follow natural language instructions and generalize across diverse tasks, but they remain vulnerable to execution failures that compromise reliability in real-world deployment. Detecting such failures during execution is therefore critical for the robust deployment of embodied systems. Existing failure detection methods either rely on expensive action resampling or external models, while alternatives propagate trajectory-level labels uniformly across every timestep, obscuring localized failure signals. In this paper, we propose \textbf{Hide-and-Seek}, a framework that formulates VLA failure detection as a coarsely supervised learning problem. By combining inter-trajectory and intra-trajectory contrastive objectives, Hide-and-Seek localizes failure-indicative actions and induces temporally structured failure signals from trajectory-level supervision alone, without any step-level annotation. We evaluate Hide-and-Seek on LIBERO, VLABench, and a real-world robotic platform across three representative VLA policies: OpenVLA, $π_0$, and $π_{0.5}$.Our method achieves state-of-the-art multi-task failure detection performance with a practical accuracy--timeliness trade-off under conformal prediction, and generalizes well to both seen and unseen tasks.

AI.tldr: Hide-and-Seek is a framework that detects execution failures in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models using only trajectory-level supervision. It combines inter-trajectory and intra-trajectory contrastive learning to localize failure-indicative actions without step-level annotations, achieving state-of-the-art performance on LIBERO, VLABench, and real-world platforms across multiple VLA policies.
AI.motivation: VLA models are vulnerable to execution failures during real-world deployment, and existing failure detection methods are either computationally expensive (action resampling or external models) or fail to capture localized failure signals due to uniform trajectory-level label propagation.
AI.method: Hide-and-Seek formulates VLA failure detection as a coarsely supervised learning problem, combining inter-trajectory and intra-trajectory contrastive objectives to localize failure-indicative actions and induce temporally structured failure signals from trajectory-level supervision alone, without requiring step-level annotations.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art multi-task failure detection performance with a practical accuracy–timeliness trade-off under conformal prediction, and generalizes well to both seen and unseen tasks across three VLA policies (OpenVLA, π₀, π₀.₅) on LIBERO, VLABench, and a real-world robotic platform.
AI.conclusion: Hide-and-Seek provides an efficient and generalizable solution for VLA failure detection that works with only trajectory-level supervision, addressing the key limitations of prior methods while maintaining practical reliability for real-world deployment.

title: Distilling LLM Feedback for Lean Theorem Proving
summary: Post-training for reasoning models typically combines supervised fine-tuning with reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards, most commonly with GRPO. However, this algorithm suffers from sparse rewards, limited exploration, and mode collapse. Building upon recent works on self-distillation, we propose Feedback Distillation, a training method where the model is trained to match, at the token level, its own distribution conditioned on privileged feedback produced by a language model. Feedback Distillation offers token-level supervision and can inject external knowledge. Evaluating our method for Lean4 theorem-proving, we find that Feedback Distillation maintains greater diversity in generated trajectories than GRPO, yielding higher policy entropy and better pass@k scaling. The two methods are complementary: initializing GRPO from a Feedback Distillation checkpoint outperforms either method alone. All in all, our results suggest a promising avenue to improve post-training for complex reasoning.

AI.tldr: Feedback Distillation improves post-training for reasoning models by matching token-level distributions conditioned on privileged feedback from a language model, outperforming GRPO in diversity and pass@k scaling for Lean4 theorem-proving, with the two methods being complementary.
AI.motivation: GRPO (commonly used for reasoning model post-training) suffers from sparse rewards, limited exploration, and mode collapse. The authors aim to address these limitations by introducing a method that provides dense, token-level supervision and injects external knowledge.
AI.method: Feedback Distillation trains the model to match, at the token level, its own distribution conditioned on privileged feedback generated by a language model. This builds upon recent self-distillation works.
AI.result: In Lean4 theorem-proving, Feedback Distillation maintains greater trajectory diversity and higher policy entropy than GRPO, with better pass@k scaling. Initializing GRPO from a Feedback Distillation checkpoint outperforms either method alone.
AI.conclusion: Feedback Distillation and GRPO are complementary; combining them yields superior performance, suggesting a promising direction for improving post-training in complex reasoning tasks.

title: High-Load-Density Electro-Permanent Magnetic Foot with Controllable Adhesion for Quadruped Wall-Climbing Robots
comment: 10 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables; project page and videos available in the repository
summary: To enable reliable climbing locomotion of quadruped robots on ferromagnetic surfaces, this paper presents a high-load-density electro-permanent magnetic foot with controllable adhesion, featuring force-feedback circular Halbach-net electro-permanent magnet (CHN-EPM) adhesion units and a magnetization control system. Due to its three-dimensional magnetic circuit structure and flux-concentration effect, the CHN-EPM enables a distributed parallel magnetic flux path with enhanced flux utilization, resulting in reduced sensitivity to air-gap variations and allowing effective adhesion to be maintained even under partial contact conditions. The proposed CHN-EPM generates a maximum adhesion force exceeding 1000 N with a load-to-weight ratio over 200:1. A magnetization driver and a two-stage pulse current control strategy are developed to regulate the excitation current amplitude and duration, enabling accurate and reliable magnetization. By incorporating a flexible pressure sensor for contact force feedback, the system can effectively monitor attachment and detachment states, ensuring robust adhesion switching under uncertain contact conditions. The proposed system is integrated into a commercial quadruped robot (Unitree GO2), demonstrating high-load adhesion on ceiling and vertical-wall surfaces and stable locomotion on painted, perforated, and curved ferromagnetic surfaces.

AI.tldr: A high-load-density electro-permanent magnetic foot with force-feedback circular Halbach-net electro-permanent magnet (CHN-EPM) adhesion units is presented for quadruped robots climbing on ferromagnetic surfaces, achieving >1000 N adhesion force with >200:1 load-to-weight ratio and robust locomotion on challenging surfaces.
AI.motivation: To enable reliable climbing locomotion of quadruped robots on ferromagnetic surfaces, addressing challenges of high load capacity, air-gap sensitivity, and robust adhesion switching under uncertain contact conditions.
AI.method: Proposed CHN-EPM with 3D magnetic circuit and flux-concentration effect for distributed parallel magnetic flux path; two-stage pulse current control strategy for magnetization; flexible pressure sensor for contact force feedback to monitor attachment/detachment states.
AI.result: Maximum adhesion force >1000 N, load-to-weight ratio >200:1, reduced sensitivity to air-gap variations, effective adhesion under partial contact, successfully integrated into Unitree GO2 robot demonstrating high-load adhesion on ceiling/vertical walls and stable locomotion on painted, perforated, and curved ferromagnetic surfaces.
AI.conclusion: The proposed electro-permanent magnetic foot with CHN-EPM and feedback control enables reliable high-load climbing locomotion on diverse ferromagnetic surfaces for quadruped robots.

title: UniScale: Adaptive Unified Inference Scaling via Online Joint Optimization of Model Routing and Test-Time Scaling
comment: Accepted at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026)
summary: In real-world deployments of large language models (LLMs), balancing inference quality and computational cost has become a central challenge. Existing approaches tackle this trade-off along two largely independent dimensions: model routing, which switches among models of different scales to match request complexity, and test-time scaling (TTS), which adjusts inference-time compute within a fixed model for fine-grained control. However, this decoupled design introduces inherent limitations. Model routing yields coarse-grained, discrete performance changes due to the sparse set of model scales, while single-model TTS often encounters capacity ceilings and exhibits diminishing returns as compute increases. Moreover, treating the two mechanisms separately restricts adaptability in dynamic inference environments. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Unified Inference Scaling (UIS), which unifies model routing and TTS in a single optimization space. Building on this formulation, we propose UniScale, an online framework that models adaptive UIS as a contextual multi-armed bandit problem and learns inference policies via LinUCB. The framework incorporates efficiency-aware learning and cost modeling to ensure stable and scalable optimization over high-dimensional action spaces. Evaluation shows that UniScale effectively exploits the synergy in the UIS space to deliver a fine-grained and consistently better quality-cost trade-off across diverse, dynamic inference scenarios.

AI.tldr: UniScale unifies model routing and test-time scaling into a single optimization framework using contextual bandits (LinUCB) to achieve finer-grained, more efficient quality-cost trade-offs in LLM inference.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches treat model routing and test-time scaling as independent mechanisms, leading to coarse-grained discrete performance, capacity ceilings, diminishing returns, and limited adaptability in dynamic inference environments.
AI.method: Introduces Unified Inference Scaling (UIS) to combine model routing and TTS into one optimization space, and proposes UniScale, an online framework formulated as a contextual multi-armed bandit problem solved via LinUCB with efficiency-aware learning and cost modeling.
AI.result: UniScale effectively exploits synergy in the UIS space, delivering fine-grained and consistently better quality-cost trade-offs across diverse, dynamic inference scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Unifying model routing and test-time scaling enables more adaptive and efficient LLM inference than treating them separately.

title: Wall-OSS-0.5 Technical Report
summary: Large-scale Vision-Language-Action (VLA) pretraining is increasingly adopted as the foundation for robot policies, yet the evidence for pretrained VLAs is almost invariably reported after task-specific fine-tuning.This leaves a foundational question unanswered: does VLA pretraining itself yield executable robot behavior, or does it merely furnish a better initialization for downstream policy learning? We present Wall-OSS-0.5, an open-source 4B VLA built upon a 3B VLM backbone augmented with action-generation components, designed so that pretrained robotic capability is directly measurable on physical hardware.The model is pretrained across more than 20 embodiments, processing over one million robot trajectories per epoch alongside a grounded multimodal corpus. We adopt a gradient-bridged co-training recipe in which three objectives play distinct and complementary roles: discrete action prediction routes strong VLM-native gradients into the backbone, multimodal prediction preserves grounded vision-language understanding, and continuous flow matching serves as the deployment-time action interface. Before task-specific fine-tuning, the pretrained checkpoint achieves non-trivial zero-shot real-robot behavior, completing several tasks, including a held-out deformable manipulation task, at high task progress on a 17-task suite. After fine-tuning, the same checkpoint serves as a stronger adaptation prior, reaching 60.5% average task progress on 15 real-robot tasks and outperforming π_0.5 by 17.5%. Multimodal evaluations further confirm that action training does not erode grounded vision-language competence: the model preserves broad vision-language ability while strengthening embodied grounding. Together, these results reposition VLA pretraining from an initialization strategy to a directly testable, already useful source of robot capability.

AI.tldr: Wall-OSS-0.5, a 4B open-source VLA model pretrained on 20+ embodiments and 1M+ trajectories, achieves zero-shot real-robot behavior before any fine-tuning and serves as a stronger adaptation prior after fine-tuning (60.5% task progress, outperforming π_0.5 by 17.5%), demonstrating that VLA pretraining itself yields executable robot capability, not just better initialization.
AI.motivation: To answer whether VLA pretraining itself yields executable robot behavior or merely provides a better initialization for downstream fine-tuning.
AI.method: A 4B VLA built on a 3B VLM backbone with action-generation components, pretrained on 20+ embodiments and 1M+ robot trajectories per epoch using a gradient-bridged co-training recipe with three objectives: discrete action prediction (for VLM-native gradients), multimodal prediction (for grounded VL understanding), and continuous flow matching (for deployment-time action interface).
AI.result: Zero-shot real-robot behavior on multiple tasks before fine-tuning; 60.5% average task progress on 15 real-robot tasks after fine-tuning, outperforming π_0.5 by 17.5%; preserved multimodal grounding without erosion of vision-language competence.
AI.conclusion: VLA pretraining should be repositioned from an initialization strategy to a directly testable, already useful source of robot capability.

title: BilliardPhys-Bench: Benchmarking Physical Reasoning and Visual Dynamics of Multimodal LLMs
summary: Current multimodal models handle static image recognition well, but intuitive physical reasoning remains a weakness. Predicting how objects will move and interact from a single image is still difficult for these systems. We present BilliardPhys-Bench, a benchmark for physical reasoning in synthetic billiards environments. Its procedural engine generates randomized scenarios with friction and elastic collisions. The benchmark tests three abilities: (1) predicting ball-to-ball collisions, (2) reasoning about wall bounces, and (3) estimating final ball positions after motion stops. We evaluate recent MLLMs from the GPT, Claude, Gemini, and Qwen families. Performance drops as simulation time increases and scene geometry grows more complex. We also observe a consistent failure mode we call "stasis bias": when the correct physical outcome is harder to infer, models tend to predict no interaction. These findings show where current MLLMs break down on visual dynamics and point toward the need for better physical inductive biases in multimodal architectures.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces BilliardPhys-Bench, a synthetic billiards benchmark for testing physical reasoning in multimodal LLMs. It reveals that models struggle with longer simulations and complex scenes, and exhibit a "stasis bias"—predicting no interaction when unsure. This highlights the need for better physical inductive biases in multimodal architectures.
AI.motivation: Multimodal models handle static image recognition well but struggle with intuitive physical reasoning, such as predicting object motion and interactions from a single image. There is a lack of systematic benchmarks to evaluate these capabilities.
AI.method: The authors build BilliardPhys-Bench using a procedural engine that generates randomized billiards scenarios with friction and elastic collisions. The benchmark tests three abilities: predicting ball-to-ball collisions, reasoning about wall bounces, and estimating final ball positions. They evaluate GPT, Claude, Gemini, and Qwen family models.
AI.result: Model performance degrades with longer simulation times and more complex scene geometry. A consistent failure mode called "stasis bias" is observed: when the correct physical outcome is hard to infer, models default to predicting no interaction.
AI.conclusion: Current MLLMs break down on visual dynamics tasks, and better physical inductive biases are needed in multimodal architectures to improve physical reasoning.

title: Trajectory Planning for Non-Communicating Mobile Robots using Inverse Optimal Control
summary: To enable an efficient interaction of non-communicating mobile robots in collision avoidance scenarios, we present a novel combined trajectory planning and prediction algorithm. Inverse optimal control is used to estimate unknown goal states of all robots based on observed past trajectories. Each robot also takes the perspective of other robots in considering self-prediction and solves a joint prediction problem using the estimated goal states. The resulting predictions are then considered for planning. Simulation results of scenarios with 2-8 robots show that the median of the durations until all vehicles reach their goals is 9.8 % faster compared to planning with constant acceleration based estimated goal states. Moreover, the proposed approach never leads to the solver being unable to find a solution to the planning or prediction problem.

AI.tldr: A combined trajectory planning and prediction algorithm using inverse optimal control to estimate goal states of non-communicating mobile robots, achieving 9.8% faster median goal-reaching times compared to constant acceleration baseline with no solver failures.
AI.motivation: To enable efficient interaction of non-communicating mobile robots in collision avoidance scenarios by improving goal state estimation and joint prediction.
AI.method: Uses inverse optimal control to estimate unknown goal states of all robots from observed past trajectories, incorporates self-prediction from each robot's perspective, solves a joint prediction problem with estimated goal states, then uses predictions for planning.
AI.result: In simulations with 2-8 robots, median goal-reaching durations were 9.8% faster compared to planning with constant acceleration-based estimated goal states, and the approach never caused solver failures.
AI.conclusion: The proposed inverse optimal control-based prediction and planning method improves efficiency and reliability in multi-robot collision avoidance without inter-robot communication.

title: A Persona-Based Evaluation Framework for Pluralistic Alignment in Generative AI
summary: Current alignment paradigms for generative artificial intelligence rely predominantly on monolithic benchmarking frameworks that reduce the plurality of human judgment to aggregated statistical baselines, thereby obscuring cultural, demographic, and contextual variability in evaluation. We introduce a state-space constrained emulation framework for AI evaluation that replaces singular assessment functions with a structured manifold of synthetic cognitive profiles representing diverse human perspectives. We show that modern generative architectures can instantiate and maintain these evaluative personas with high consistency, enabling a form of pluralistic, perspective-dependent benchmarking that more closely reflects real-world consensus variability. However, we further analyze the stability of these simulated evaluators under sequential inference and stochastic prompt perturbations, revealing systematic degradation in persona coherence that manifests as state-space drift and semantic inconsistency. These findings suggest that static alignment constraints are insufficient for sustaining robust evaluative behavior over time. Instead, we argue for the necessity of embedding dynamic, viability-driven regulatory mechanisms within generative systems to preserve coherent cognitive emulation. By framing persona-based evaluation as a structured dynamical system over latent representation manifolds, this study provides a foundation for more adaptive, human-aligned, and context-sensitive approaches to AI evaluation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a pluralistic AI evaluation framework using synthetic cognitive profiles (evaluative personas) to replace monolithic benchmarks, but finds that persona coherence degrades over time due to state-space drift, arguing for dynamic regulatory mechanisms to sustain robust evaluation.
AI.motivation: Current AI evaluation relies on monolithic benchmarks that aggregate human judgments into statistical baselines, obscuring cultural, demographic, and contextual variability. The authors seek a more pluralistic, perspective-dependent approach that reflects real-world consensus diversity.
AI.method: A state-space constrained emulation framework is introduced, where a manifold of synthetic cognitive profiles (evaluative personas) is instantiated and maintained by generative architectures. Persona consistency is analyzed under sequential inference and stochastic prompt perturbations to assess stability.
AI.result: Generative models can instantiate and maintain evaluative personas with high consistency, enabling pluralistic benchmarking. However, systematic degradation—state-space drift and semantic inconsistency—occurs under sequential inference and prompt perturbations, indicating that static alignment constraints are insufficient.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, viability-driven regulatory mechanisms are necessary to preserve coherent cognitive emulation. Persona-based evaluation should be framed as a structured dynamical system over latent representation manifolds, leading to more adaptive, human-aligned, and context-sensitive AI evaluation.

title: Enhancing Human-Likeness in Reinforcement Learning Agents via Hierarchical Macro Action Quantization
summary: Human-like agents are a long-standing goal of artificial intelligence. Despite strong performance, most reinforcement learning (RL) agents remain reward-driven and often exhibit behaviors that differ from humans, limiting interpretability and reliability. In this work, we introduce a novel human-like RL framework that predicts action sequences closely aligned with human behaviors while maximizing rewards. Specifically, we encode human demonstrations into macro actions using a hierarchical macro action quantization approach (termed HiMAQ) consisting of two successive levels of vector quantization. The lower quantization level maps input actions to fine-grained subaction clusters, while the higher quantization level aggregates these subaction clusters into action clusters. Extensive evaluations on the D4RL benchmarks show that our hierarchical approach outperforms the non-hierarchical baseline (MAQ), achieving better human-likeness scores while maintaining comparable or better success rates than previous RL agents. The improvements generalize across integrations with various RL algorithms, namely IQL, SAC, and RLPD.

AI.tldr: HiMAQ is a hierarchical macro action quantization framework that encodes human demonstrations into macro actions through two-level vector quantization, enabling RL agents to predict human-like action sequences while maximizing rewards, achieving better human-likeness scores and comparable/better success rates than baselines across multiple RL algorithms.
AI.motivation: Existing RL agents remain reward-driven and exhibit behaviors that differ from humans, limiting interpretability and reliability. The goal is to create human-like RL agents that align with human behaviors while still maximizing rewards.
AI.method: A hierarchical macro action quantization (HiMAQ) framework with two successive levels of vector quantization: a lower level maps input actions to fine-grained subaction clusters, and a higher level aggregates these subaction clusters into action clusters, encoding human demonstrations into macro actions for RL agents.
AI.result: HiMAQ outperforms the non-hierarchical baseline (MAQ) on D4RL benchmarks, achieving better human-likeness scores with comparable or better success rates than previous RL agents. Improvements generalize across IQL, SAC, and RLPD integrations.
AI.conclusion: The proposed hierarchical approach effectively bridges the gap between human-like behavior and reward maximization in RL, offering improved interpretability and reliability while maintaining competitive task performance.

title: HADT: A Heterogeneous Multi-Agent Differential Transformer for Autonomous Earth Observation Satellite Cluster
comment: Accepted in ECML-PKDD 2026. arXiv admin note: text overlap with arXiv:2511.12792
summary: This work addresses the problem of autonomous resource management in heterogeneous satellite cluster conducting Earth Observation (EO) missions including optical and Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) satellites. In autonomous operation mode, satellites are equipped with intelligent capabilities enabling real-time decision-making based on the latest conditions, while requiring minimal interaction with ground operators. Traditional scheduling approaches typically rely on mathematical models to represent satellite mission and resource management. Then, this problem is solved by using optimization algorithms. However, such solutions become less effective when the underlying models are not available, over complex, and inaccurate due to dynamic changes and uncertainties inherent in the space mission environment. A promising alternative is to reformulate the problem as a sequential decision-making process and apply model-free reinforcement learning techniques to enable adaptive and real-time resource management. To this end, we propose a novel transformer-based architecture tailored for heterogeneous satellite cluster autonomous EO Mission with relational observations-actions tokenization and differential attention mechanism. Our experimental results demonstrate significant performance improvements compared to the available baselines. Moreover, the proposed architecture exhibits strong adaptability and transferability with respect to varying numbers of satellite clusters.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a transformer-based reinforcement learning architecture for autonomous resource management in heterogeneous satellite clusters (optical + SAR) conducting Earth Observation missions. The approach uses relational observations-actions tokenization and differential attention to enable adaptive, real-time decision-making without relying on explicit mathematical models, outperforming traditional optimization-based baselines and showing strong adaptability to varying cluster sizes.
AI.motivation: Traditional optimization-based scheduling approaches for satellite resource management become ineffective when underlying models are unavailable, overly complex, or inaccurate due to dynamic uncertainties in space environments. The authors aim to overcome these limitations by reformulating the problem as a sequential decision-making process using model-free reinforcement learning.
AI.method: A novel transformer-based architecture is proposed for heterogeneous satellite clusters (optical and SAR). It features relational observations-actions tokenization and a differential attention mechanism, enabling the model to handle varying numbers of satellite agents and learn adaptive resource management policies via model-free reinforcement learning.
AI.result: The proposed architecture demonstrates significant performance improvements over available baselines, along with strong adaptability and transferability across different numbers of satellite clusters.
AI.conclusion: Transformer-based RL with relational tokenization and differential attention is a promising approach for autonomous, model-free resource management in heterogeneous satellite EO missions, offering robustness to dynamic uncertainties and scalability to varying cluster configurations.

title: RDGen: Demonstration Generation for High-Quality Robot Learning via Reinforcement Learning
comment: 13 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose robot control. However, their performance remains fundamentally constrained by the availability of high-quality robot trajectory data. In current robot learning practice, such data are primarily collected through human teleoperation, which is labor-intensive, costly, and difficult to scale. In this paper, we propose RDGen, a sim-to-real reinforcement learning framework for generating high-quality robot demonstrations. Rather than employing reinforcement learning solely as the final control policy, RDGen leverages trained RL policies as a structured trajectory generator. The system consists of a VLM-based task parser that identifies task-relevant objects, a Grounding DINO-based object localizer, and an RL policy transferred from simulation to the real robot. Successful rollouts are then harvested as clean, high-quality demonstrations for downstream VLA training, while the simulation stage further provides a scalable source of additional trajectories at little marginal cost. Experiments on a pick-and-place task demonstrate that the transferred RL policy achieves a high task success rate. Compared with human teleoperation, RDGen produces significantly smoother trajectories and yields superior downstream VLA performance. These results indicate that RL-generated demonstrations can serve as more reliable and consistent supervisory signals for robot policy learning.

AI.tldr: RDGen is a sim-to-real RL framework that generates high-quality robot demonstrations by using trained RL policies as structured trajectory generators, outperforming human teleoperation for downstream VLA model training on pick-and-place tasks.
AI.motivation: VLA models for robot control are limited by the scarcity of high-quality robot trajectory data, which is currently collected through labor-intensive and costly human teleoperation that is difficult to scale.
AI.method: RDGen uses a VLM-based task parser for object identification, a Grounding DINO-based object localizer, and an RL policy transferred from simulation to real robots. Successful rollouts are harvested as demonstrations for downstream VLA training, with simulation providing additional scalable trajectories.
AI.result: The transferred RL policy achieves high task success rate on pick-and-place tasks, produces significantly smoother trajectories than human teleoperation, and yields superior downstream VLA performance.
AI.conclusion: RL-generated demonstrations can serve as more reliable and consistent supervisory signals for robot policy learning compared to human teleoperation.

title: GraphARC: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Graph-Based Abstract Reasoning
comment: Accepted at KDD 2026 Datasets and Benchmarks Track
summary: Relational reasoning lies at the heart of intelligence, but existing benchmarks are typically confined to formats such as grids or text. We introduce GraphARC, a benchmark for abstract reasoning on graph-structured data. GraphARC generalizes the few-shot transformation learning paradigm of the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC). Each task requires inferring a transformation rule from a few input-output pairs and applying it to a new test graph, covering local, global, and hierarchical graph transformations. Unlike grid-based ARC, GraphARC instances can be generated at scale across diverse graph families and sizes, enabling systematic evaluation of generalization abilities. We evaluate state-of-the-art language models on GraphARC and observe clear limitations. Models can answer questions about graph properties but often fail to solve the full graph transformation task, revealing a comprehension-execution gap. Performance further degrades on larger instances, exposing scaling barriers. More broadly, by combining aspects of node classification, link prediction, and graph generation within a single framework, GraphARC provides a promising testbed for future graph foundation models.

AI.tldr: GraphARC is a new benchmark for abstract reasoning on graph-structured data that generalizes ARC's transformation learning paradigm, revealing that language models can understand graph properties but fail at executing full graph transformations, especially on larger instances.
AI.motivation: Existing abstract reasoning benchmarks are limited to grid or text formats; there is a need for graph-structured abstract reasoning evaluation that can be generated at scale across diverse graph families to systematically test generalization.
AI.method: GraphARC generalizes the few-shot transformation learning paradigm from ARC to graphs, requiring models to infer transformation rules from input-output pairs and apply them to new test graphs, covering local, global, and hierarchical graph transformations.
AI.result: State-of-the-art language models can answer questions about graph properties but struggle with full graph transformation tasks, exposing a comprehension-execution gap; performance degrades on larger instances, revealing scaling barriers.
AI.conclusion: GraphARC provides a unified framework combining node classification, link prediction, and graph generation, serving as a promising testbed for future graph foundation models to bridge the comprehension-execution gap and improve scaling abilities.

title: A study on a Real-Time VR-Based Teleoperation Framework for Manipulator in Dynamic Environment
comment: This manuscript has been submitted for possible publication
summary: Robot teleoperation enables safe, non-contact task execution in hazardous environments where direct human access is difficult, and its application has expanded with recent VR technologies. Many VR teleoperation studies, however, have primarily served as data-collection tools for robot imitation learning, so they often do not explicitly address dynamic obstacles, workspace changes, or collision risks during operation. For real deployment aimed at operator safety, teleoperation must react to dynamic situations with low latency and remain robust to mistakes made by inexperienced operators. This paper presents a VR teleoperation framework that supports real-time manipulation while handling collisions with both static and moving obstacles. The framework integrates GPU-accelerated inverse kinematics and trajectory optimization within a VR interface to generate feasible joint commands at each control cycle under robot constraints. Experiments with a 7-DoF manipulator demonstrate stable online behavior and collision-aware motion generation across three scenarios: obstacle-free, static-obstacle, and moving-obstacle environments. The results indicate that the proposed approach generates motion consistent with the operator's command while producing safe detours when obstacles interfere with the commanded path.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a VR teleoperation framework that integrates GPU-accelerated inverse kinematics and trajectory optimization to enable real-time, collision-aware manipulation for both static and moving obstacles, demonstrated on a 7-DoF manipulator across three scenarios.
AI.motivation: Existing VR teleoperation systems are primarily used as data-collection tools for imitation learning and lack explicit handling of dynamic obstacles, workspace changes, and collision risks, which are critical for real deployment and operator safety.
AI.method: The framework integrates GPU-accelerated inverse kinematics and trajectory optimization within a VR interface, generating feasible joint commands under robot constraints at each control cycle with low latency.
AI.result: Experiments with a 7-DoF manipulator demonstrate stable online behavior and collision-aware motion generation in obstacle-free, static-obstacle, and moving-obstacle environments.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach generates motion consistent with the operator's command while producing safe detours when obstacles interfere with the commanded path.

title: Vector Linking via Cross-Model Local Isometric Consistency
comment: Accepted at ICML 2026
summary: We study Vector Linking: given two embedding clouds produced by different black-box encoders over partially overlapping datasets, recover cross-model object correspondences using only vectors. Empirically and theoretically, we show that independently trained contrastive encoders exhibit local geometric consistency: short-range distances are approximately preserved up to a scale factor, while long-range distances are not due to model-specific distortion. Building on this, we propose an iterative, reference-based geometric embedding hashing that recovers vector links from a tiny seed set of paired anchors. It represents each vector by distances to sampled paired anchors, proposes candidate links via hash-space matching, and aggregates evidence across views in a Beta-Bernoulli posterior to bootstrap high-confidence links as new anchors. Experiments across multiple benchmarks and embedding model pairs demonstrate accurate and robust linking under varying overlap, seed budgets, and out-of-domain anchors, with applications to vector database integration and cross-model clustering. Code is available at https://github.com/DBgroup-Edinburgh/VecLinking.

AI.tldr: A method called Vector Linking recovers cross-model object correspondences between two embedding clouds from different black-box encoders by exploiting local geometric consistency and using an iterative reference-based hashing scheme with a small seed set of paired anchors.
AI.motivation: Different black-box embedding models produce incompatible vector spaces, making it difficult to link corresponding objects across them without direct model access or shared training data.
AI.method: Proposes iterative reference-based geometric embedding hashing: represents each vector by distances to sampled paired anchors, matches in hash space, and uses a Beta-Bernoulli posterior to bootstrap high-confidence links as new anchors.
AI.result: Demonstrates accurate and robust linking across multiple benchmarks and model pairs under varying overlap, seed budgets, and out-of-domain anchors.
AI.conclusion: Local geometric consistency is preserved across independently trained contrastive encoders, enabling effective cross-model linking with applications to vector database integration and cross-model clustering.

title: Can Aerial VLA Models Cooperate? Evaluating Closed-Loop Air-Ground Coordination with CARLA-Air
comment: Code at https://github.com/louiszengCN/CarlaAir
summary:
Recent aerial vision-language-action (VLA) models show promising single-UAV capabilities, such as tracking moving objects and navigating to language-specified landmarks. However, it remains unclear whether these capabilities can transfer to air-ground cooperation, where a UAV and a UGV must act jointly in a shared, closed-loop physical world.
  We study this question with CARLA-Air, a single-process air-ground evaluation environment that unifies CARLA and AirSim inside one Unreal Engine runtime. By sharing the same world state, physics tick, and sensing pipeline, CARLA-Air enables physically consistent UAV--UGV interaction and precise measurement of simulation-timestamp alignment and effective coordination latency.
  Using CARLA-Air, we evaluate representative aerial VLA and planning baselines on two complementary diagnostic tasks: moving-platform landing and occlusion-recovery escort. The results show that current aerial VLA models can often track or follow a ground partner, but struggle to convert this single-agent competence into stable cooperative behavior. State prompting provides limited benefit, and naive bidirectional interaction fails to consistently improve performance and can amplify errors for most baselines. These findings suggest that, under the tested text-based cue interfaces, zero-shot cooperative air-ground VLA requires three components beyond the current paradigm: explicit partner-state grounding, low-latency action coordination, and team-level objective alignment. Our code is available at https://github.com/louiszengCN/CarlaAir.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces CARLA-Air, a unified simulation environment for air-ground cooperation, and shows that current aerial VLA models (designed for single-UAV tasks) fail to achieve stable cooperative behavior with UGVs, requiring explicit partner grounding, low-latency coordination, and team-level objective alignment.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether single-UAV aerial VLA capabilities can transfer to air-ground cooperation scenarios where a UAV and UGV must jointly act in a shared closed-loop physical world.
AI.method: Develops CARLA-Air, a single-process evaluation environment unifying CARLA and AirSim in one Unreal Engine runtime for physically consistent UAV-UGV interaction. Evaluates aerial VLA and planning baselines on moving-platform landing and occlusion-recovery escort tasks.
AI.result: Aerial VLA models can track/follow ground partners but struggle to convert single-agent competence into stable cooperative behavior. State prompting offers limited benefit; naive bidirectional interaction does not consistently improve performance and can amplify errors for most baselines.
AI.conclusion: Zero-shot cooperative air-ground VLA under text-based cue interfaces requires three components beyond the current paradigm: explicit partner-state grounding, low-latency action coordination, and team-level objective alignment.

title: LLM-FACETS: A Privacy-Preserving Framework for Evaluating LLM Transparency and Accountability
comment: Submitted to ACM Journal on Responsible Computing, Special Section: Collaborative Methods and Tools for Engineering and Evaluating Transparency in AI. 28 pages 9 figures, 7 tables, 1 algorithm. Source code: https://github.com/Scriptor-Group/AIMVi
summary: Assessing whether Large Language Models outputs are factually grounded, epistemically calibrated, and methodologically reproducible is a prerequisite for responsible AI deployment. Yet auditing LLMs remains inaccessible to non-technical practitioners: existing tools require programming expertise and non-trivial environment setup, and cloud-hosted platforms transmit evaluation data to external services, creating barriers for domain experts and compliance officers legally responsible for AI oversight. We introduce LLM-FACETS (LLM FActuality Cross-EvaluaTion System): an open-source framework with a browser-accessible interface and a plugin architecture, structured around three practitioner profiles (technical experts, domain experts, compliance officers) that mirror the stakeholder categories identified in the EU AI Act and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework. The architecture makes data flows explicit: deterministic metrics (BLEU, ROUGE, BERTScore) run entirely within the self-hosted server with no outbound transmission; LLM-judge metrics contact external APIs explicitly, with users retaining full credential control. The framework operationalizes transparency through three mechanisms: token-level log-probability visualization for epistemic uncertainty, multi-judge consensus to mitigate judge bias, and RAG Triad metrics (Faithfulness, Answer Relevance, Context Relevance) to detect and localize hallucinations. A plugin architecture allows any new metric or dataset to be integrated without modifying the evaluation pipeline. The open-source implementation enables cross-checking across multiple metrics targeting the same property, ensuring reproducibility and decoupling AI accountability from the teams building the systems assessed. We verify the framework through cross-validation of 18 metric implementations against canonical reference libraries.

AI.tldr: LLM-FACETS is an open-source, browser-accessible framework for auditing LLMs that supports three practitioner profiles (technical experts, domain experts, compliance officers), runs deterministic metrics locally, makes LLM-judge API calls transparent, and provides plugin architecture for extensible, reproducible evaluation.
AI.motivation: Current LLM auditing tools require programming expertise and complex setup, and cloud platforms transmit data externally, making factual grounding, epistemic calibration, and reproducibility checks inaccessible to non-technical practitioners like domain experts and compliance officers who are legally responsible for AI oversight under regulations such as the EU AI Act and NIST AI Risk Management Framework.
AI.method: The framework provides a browser-accessible interface with a plugin architecture structured around three practitioner profiles. Deterministic metrics (BLEU, ROUGE, BERTScore) run locally; LLM-judge metrics contact external APIs explicitly with user credential control. Transparency is operationalized via token-level log-probability visualization, multi-judge consensus, and RAG Triad metrics. Cross-validation against 18 canonical metric implementations was performed.
AI.result: The framework was verified through cross-validation of 18 metric implementations against canonical reference libraries, confirming correctness and reproducibility.
AI.conclusion: LLM-FACETS makes LLM auditing accessible to non-technical stakeholders, ensures data flow transparency, enables reproducibility through multi-metric cross-checking, and decouples AI accountability from system-building teams, supporting regulatory compliance.

title: Seeing Fast and Slow: Bimodal 3D Scene Graphs for Open-set Tasks
summary: Open-set task execution can significantly benefit from seamlessly switching between coarse and fine scene representations depending on the context and the evolving information as the robot explores the environment. For example, it is often sufficient to start with a coarse scene representation initially and only employ a finer, more granular scene representation when the robot encounters regions which are likely to contain the task relevant objects. Hence, in this work, we propose BiMoSG, a bimodal 3D scene graph generation approach for open-set tasks. BiMoSG employs a "fast" mode by default to efficiently generate a coarse 3D scene graph and can switch to a "slow" mode for generating a finer open vocabulary 3D scene graph of task relevant objects. We demonstrate that our proposed 3D scene graph generation approach is significantly faster than the open-source state-of-the-art approaches. This allows us to integrate the scene graph generation process with task execution for real-time deployment.

AI.tldr: BiMoSG is a bimodal 3D scene graph generation approach for open-set tasks that uses a default "fast" mode for coarse scene graphs and can switch to a "slow" mode for finer open-vocabulary graphs, achieving significantly faster performance than state-of-the-art methods and enabling real-time integration with task execution.
AI.motivation: Open-set task execution benefits from dynamically switching between coarse and fine scene representations based on context, avoiding unnecessary computational overhead by using coarse representations initially and finer ones only when task-relevant regions are encountered.
AI.method: BiMoSG operates in two modes: a default "fast" mode for efficient coarse 3D scene graph generation, and a "slow" mode for generating finer open vocabulary 3D scene graphs of task-relevant objects, with seamless switching between the two based on contextual needs.
AI.result: The proposed approach is significantly faster than open-source state-of-the-art 3D scene graph generation methods, enabling integration of scene graph generation with task execution for real-time deployment.
AI.conclusion: BiMoSG enables real-time open-set task execution by efficiently switching between coarse and fine scene representations, outperforming existing approaches in speed while maintaining the flexibility needed for open-vocabulary tasks.

title: Formalizing and falsifying causal pathways of rare events
comment: accepted for ICML 2026
summary: Building on recent formalizations of root cause analysis for rare events (``outliers'') in structural equation models, we propose a formal definition of a causal pathway and discuss its testable implications. We identify conditions under which these implications depend only on a causal abstraction defined by the pathway of rare events, rather than on the full causal graph of the underlying system. Accordingly, we introduce an abstraction of causal structure to pathways of rare events that bridges simple verbal causal explanations and detailed causal modeling.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes causal pathway definitions for rare events (outliers) in structural equation models, showing that testable implications can depend only on pathway abstraction rather than the full causal graph, bridging verbal explanations and detailed causal modeling.
AI.motivation: To formalize root cause analysis for rare events (outliers) in structural equation models by defining causal pathways and their testable implications.
AI.method: Formal definition of causal pathways, analysis of testable implications under causal abstraction, and introduction of an abstraction mechanism that bridges verbal explanations and detailed causal modeling.
AI.result: Identified conditions where testable implications depend only on the causal abstraction defined by the pathway of rare events, not the full causal graph.
AI.conclusion: Introduced an abstraction of causal structure to pathways of rare events that bridges simple verbal causal explanations and detailed causal modeling.

title: Building Generalization Into Behavior Generation Via Adaptive Compositions of Regularities
comment: 10 pages, 6 figures
summary: Generalization in robotics requires prior knowledge about how the world is structured, yet this structure changes from one situation to the next. This paper investigates the proposition that generalization arises from adaptively composing regularities -- predictable relationships within the robot-environment system -- into situation-appropriate structures for behavior generation. We examine this proposition by analyzing the mechanism in AICON (Active InterCONnect), a framework representing regularities as interacting processes in a differentiable network, where sensory feedback realizes composition and gradient descent generates behavior. To isolate adaptive composition as the key mechanism, we study a simple simulated problem in which all relevant regularities can be identified. We expose the resulting model to a wide range of novel conditions not considered during design, and we find that it generates context-appropriate behavior in all but one case, where encoded regularities are provably insufficient. Ablations reveal that the network automatically modulates which regularities influence behavior based on their informativeness. These results suggest that adaptive composition of regularities constitutes a powerful inductive bias for building generalization into behavior generation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes that generalization in robotics arises from adaptively composing regularities (predictable relationships) into situation-appropriate structures. Using the AICON framework, where regularities are represented as interacting processes in a differentiable network with sensory feedback and gradient descent, the model generates context-appropriate behavior under novel conditions. Results show the network automatically modulates regularity influence based on informativeness, suggesting adaptive composition is a powerful inductive bias for generalization.
AI.motivation: To investigate how generalization in robotics can be achieved through adaptive composition of regularities, given that world structure changes across situations and prior knowledge is needed but must be flexibly applied.
AI.method: The paper analyzes the AICON (Active InterCONnect) framework, which represents regularities as interacting processes in a differentiable network. Sensory feedback realizes composition and gradient descent generates behavior. The mechanism is isolated by studying a simple simulated problem where all relevant regularities can be identified, and the model is tested under novel conditions not considered during design.
AI.result: The model generates context-appropriate behavior under a wide range of novel conditions in all but one case, where encoded regularities were provably insufficient. Ablations show the network automatically modulates which regularities influence behavior based on their informativeness.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive composition of regularities constitutes a powerful inductive bias for building generalization into behavior generation in robotics.

title: COLLEAGUE.SKILL: Automated AI Skill Generation via Expert Knowledge Distillation
comment: 12 pages, 4 figures
summary: LLM agents are increasingly expected not only to complete isolated tasks, but also to carry bounded representations of human expertise, judgment, and interaction style. Building such person-grounded agents remains difficult because actionable knowledge associated with a person or role is usually embedded in heterogeneous traces rather than written as clean instructions. Existing memory and persona systems capture fragments of this evidence, while skill frameworks provide portable packaging formats; however, there is no end-to-end workflow for distilling these traces into inspectable, correctable, and agent-usable skills. We present an automated trace-to-skill distillation system for generating person-grounded AI skills via expert knowledge distillation. Given materials from a target person or role, COLLEAGUE.SKILL produces a versioned skill package with two coordinated tracks: a capability track for practices, mental models, and decision heuristics, and a bounded behavior track for communication style, interaction rules, and correction history. The package can be inspected, invoked, updated through natural-language feedback, rolled back, installed across agent hosts, and optionally prepared for controlled distribution. We describe the artifact contract, generation workflow, correction lifecycle, deployment surface, and domain presets implemented in the open-source system. At the time of writing, the public repository has approximately 18.5k GitHub stars; the gallery lists 215 skills from 165 contributors and more than 100k cumulative stars across listed skill cards. The system illustrates how person-grounded skills can be represented as portable, correctable packages rather than opaque prompts or hidden memories.

AI.tldr: COLLEAGUE.SKILL is an open-source system that automatically distills heterogeneous traces (materials from a target person or role) into versioned, inspectable, correctable skill packages for LLM agents. Each package contains a capability track (practices, mental models, decision heuristics) and a bounded behavior track (communication style, interaction rules, correction history). The system supports inspection, natural-language updates, rollback, multi-host deployment, and controlled distribution. The public repository has ~18.5k GitHub stars; the gallery lists 215 skills from 165 contributors with >100k cumulative stars.
AI.motivation: LLM agents need bounded representations of human expertise, judgment, and interaction style, but actionable knowledge about a person or role is typically embedded in heterogeneous traces rather than clean instructions. Existing memory/persona systems capture fragments, and skill frameworks provide portable formats, but no end-to-end workflow exists for distilling these traces into inspectable, correctable, and agent-usable skills.
AI.method: An automated trace-to-skill distillation system that, given materials from a target person or role, produces a versioned skill package with two coordinated tracks: (1) a capability track for practices, mental models, and decision heuristics; and (2) a bounded behavior track for communication style, interaction rules, and correction history. The system includes an artifact contract, generation workflow, correction lifecycle, deployment surface, and domain presets implemented as open-source software.
AI.result: The public repository has ~18.5k GitHub stars; the gallery contains 215 skills from 165 contributors with >100k cumulative stars across listed skill cards.
AI.conclusion: Person-grounded skills can be effectively represented as portable, correctable packages (rather than opaque prompts or hidden memories), enabling inspection, natural-language correction, rollback, multi-host deployment, and controlled distribution.

title: Don't Fool Me Twice: Adapting to Adversity in the Wild with Experience-Driven Reasoning
summary: In robotics, dangers and adversity modes are often embodiment-specific and relative to each agent. A frontier of autonomous mobile robotics is to enable agents to operate effectively in the wild in unseen unstructured environments. A significant challenge in unseen unstructured environments is that it may not be possible to predict all the dangers to the specific robot. Although recent work has used large foundation vision-language models (VLMs) to preemptively predict an exhaustive list of common-sense dangers, it remains difficult to capture possible interaction and embodiment-dependent adversities. We propose a continual learning framework for a mobile embodied agent to learn online from disturbances and attribute anomalous behaviours to causes through semantics, enabling better prediction and planning of the world in the future. Our framework, "Don't Fool Me Twice", first observes disturbances and describes their effects on the robot; this description is augmented with visual context to query a VLM to predict possible causes; the local disturbance is characterized using kernel regression, which allows for efficient, few-shot modeling of transient anomalies. We leverage semantic voxel-centric modeling to estimate epistemic uncertainty, enabling richer downstream recovery by treating interaction-driven disturbances as learnable spatial behaviors. We present four hypotheses and validate them in simulation and on hardware across embodiments and adversity modes.

AI.tldr: "Don't Fool Me Twice" proposes a continual learning framework that enables mobile robots to learn online from disturbances by using vision-language models to describe anomalies, kernel regression for few-shot modeling, and semantic voxel-based uncertainty estimation for improved prediction and planning in unseen unstructured environments.
AI.motivation: Existing VLM-based methods for danger prediction in unstructured environments struggle to capture embodiment-specific and interaction-dependent adversities that cannot be exhaustively predefined, limiting robot robustness in the wild.
AI.method: A continual learning framework with four components: (1) disturbance observation and semantic description of effects on the robot; (2) visual context augmentation to query a VLM for possible causes; (3) kernel regression for efficient few-shot characterization of transient local disturbances; (4) semantic voxel-centric modeling to estimate epistemic uncertainty, treating disturbances as learnable spatial behaviors.
AI.result: Validated across four hypotheses through both simulation and hardware experiments across different robot embodiments and adversity modes.
AI.conclusion: Online continual learning from disturbances with semantic VLM reasoning and spatial uncertainty modeling enables more robust operation in unseen unstructured environments by attributing anomalies to causes and improving future prediction/planning.

title: Industrializing Prediction-Powered Inference: The GLIDE Library for Reliable GenAI and Agentic Systems Evaluation
comment: 8 pages, accepted at the ICML 2026 workshop Agentic Uncertainty
summary: Reliable evaluation of agentic systems requires unbiased estimates with valid uncertainty, but standard practice navigates between costly human annotation and biased LLM-as-judge proxies. Prediction-powered inference (PPI) combines both into debiased estimates with valid confidence intervals, yet its various methods remain scattered across papers under partial implementations. We introduce GLIDE, an open-source Python library that unifies state-of-the-art PPI estimators (PPI++, Stratified PPI, Predict-Then-Debias and its stratified variants, Active Statistical Inference) and samplers (uniform, stratified, active, cost-optimal) under a scipy-style API specialized to mean estimation. GLIDE ships with a reproducible Monte Carlo validation suite, an empirically grounded decision tree for method selection, and an agentic evaluation case study showing substantial annotation savings at equivalent precision. The GLIDE package is available at this URL: https://github.com/EmertonData/glide

AI.tldr: GLIDE is an open-source Python library unifying state-of-the-art Prediction-Powered Inference (PPI) estimators and samplers under a scipy-style API for debiased agentic evaluation with valid confidence intervals, validated via Monte Carlo simulations and a case study showing annotation savings.
