AI.motivation: Reliable evaluation of agentic systems requires unbiased estimates with valid uncertainty, but standard practice faces a trade-off between costly human annotation and biased LLM-as-judge proxies.
AI.method: GLIDE unifies state-of-the-art PPI estimators (PPI++, Stratified PPI, Predict-Then-Debias and its stratified variants, Active Statistical Inference) and samplers (uniform, stratified, active, cost-optimal) under a scipy-style API specialized to mean estimation, ships with reproducible Monte Carlo validation, and provides an empirically grounded decision tree for method selection.
AI.result: An agentic evaluation case study showing substantial annotation savings at equivalent precision.
AI.conclusion: GLIDE enables practitioners to obtain debiased estimates with valid confidence intervals while reducing annotation cost, unifying scattered PPI methods into a practical open-source library.

title: TARIC: Memory-Augmented Traversability-Aware Outdoor VLN under Interrupted Semantic Cues
summary:
Outdoor vision-language navigation (VLN) in long-range, open-world environments is frequently disrupted by semantic-cue interruptions, where informative goal cues become sparse, occluded, or leave the field of view. Once such cues disappear, agents enter a cue-free phase and often degrade into backtracking, oscillatory headings, or aimless exploration. While memory-based methods attempt to bridge these gaps, they often fail under traversability-driven detours: the remembered cue direction may be infeasible, forcing detours that prolong cue-free phases and gradually render robot-centric cues stale and implicit histories blurred. This makes traversability a stability condition for maintaining goal-directed guidance, rather than merely a local safety concern.
  We propose a unified outdoor VLN framework that survives semantic-cue interruptions by maintaining traversability-consistent executable guidance throughout prolonged cue-free phases. Specifically, our method extracts semantic bearings from visibility-gated goal or exploration cues and grounds them into executable headings using a real-time near-field traversability profile, providing goal-consistent feasible guidance beyond reject-only safety filtering. To prevent guidance degradation during detours, we lift intermittent 2D evidence into a world-aligned 3D cue memory with an uncertainty-aware readout mechanism, ensuring guidance remains continuously reachable and stable as the robot moves.
  We evaluate the framework on quadrupedal and wheeled platforms over 600--1000 m routes. Our method improves simulation success rate by over 10 percentage points over the strongest baseline and achieves a real-world success rate of 40%, compared to 17.5% for the strongest baseline, with substantially higher robustness during prolonged cue-free intervals.

AI.tldr: A unified outdoor VLN framework that maintains traversability-consistent executable guidance during prolonged semantic-cue interruptions, using visibility-gated semantic bearings, near-field traversability profiles, and world-aligned 3D cue memory with uncertainty-aware readout, improving real-world success rate to 40% vs 17.5% baseline.
AI.motivation: Outdoor VLN agents suffer from semantic-cue interruptions (sparse/occluded goal cues) leading to backtracking, oscillation, or aimless exploration. Memory-based methods fail under traversability-driven detours, as stale cues and blurred histories degrade goal-directed guidance. Traversability is identified as a stability condition, not just a local safety concern.
AI.method: (1) Extracts semantic bearings from visibility-gated goal/exploration cues, grounded into executable headings via real-time near-field traversability profiles for goal-consistent feasible guidance. (2) Lifts intermittent 2D evidence into a world-aligned 3D cue memory with uncertainty-aware readout to maintain continuously reachable and stable guidance during detours.
AI.result: On quadrupedal and wheeled platforms over 600–1000m routes: simulation success rate improved by >10 pp over strongest baseline; real-world success rate 40% vs 17.5% baseline, with substantially higher robustness during prolonged cue-free intervals.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework effectively survives semantic-cue interruptions by maintaining traversability-consistent executable guidance, significantly outperforming baselines in both simulated and real-world long-range outdoor VLN tasks.

title: TraceGraph: Shared Decision Landscapes for Diagnosing and Improving Agent Trajectories
summary: Agent benchmarks increasingly record rich interaction trajectories, yet evaluation often reduces each rollout to a pass rate or reward score. We introduce TraceGraph, a graph-based framework that turns released multi-model agent trajectories into shared decision landscapes. For each task, TraceGraph builds a graph over observable action-observation states from pooled rollouts before model identity is introduced. It then overlays outcome-informed productive cores and trap regions, and summarizes each rollout with three events: Access, Trap exposure, and Repair. Across trajectories spanning five benchmark splits, TraceGraph profiles reveal navigation differences hidden by aggregate scores and show that splits differ in whether they reward avoiding traps or recovering from them. The same TraceGraph landscape also motivates a trap-aware recovery pipeline for SWE-bench: aruntime detector fires on states matching historical trap regions, then lightweight continuation policies are evaluated from the same prefix. On fired states, the best pooled single-factor policy raises official resolved rate from 40.4% to 43.5% on the per-provider fired subset and from 41.0% to 44.8% on common-fired instances, with provider-specific active components. Overall, TraceGraph provides a process vocabulary for asking what agent benchmarks test, where models diverge on a shared landscape, and how failure regions can guide downstream improvement.

AI.tldr: TraceGraph builds a graph from pooled multi-model agent trajectories to identify productive cores and trap regions, enabling fine-grained analysis of model behavior and a trap-aware recovery pipeline that improves SWE-bench pass rates by ~3-4%.
AI.motivation: Agent benchmarks use rich trajectories but often reduce evaluation to simple pass/reward scores, losing granular behavioral information. The paper seeks a framework to understand where models diverge and what benchmarks actually test.
AI.method: TraceGraph constructs a shared decision graph over pooled action-observation states (anonymized of model identity), identifies productive cores and trap regions via outcome labels, summarizes rollouts via three events (Access, Trap exposure, Repair), and applies a trap-aware recovery pipeline using a runtime detector and lightweight continuation policies.
AI.result: On SWE-bench, the best pooled single-factor policy raises official resolved rate from 40.4% to 43.5% on per-provider fired subset and from 41.0% to 44.8% on common-fired instances. Profiles reveal hidden navigation differences across benchmark splits.
AI.conclusion: TraceGraph provides a process-level vocabulary for analyzing what agent benchmarks test, how models differ on shared landscapes, and how failure regions can guide targeted improvement.

title: Simulation of collision avoidance behavior in crowd movement by data-driven approach
summary: Crowd movement simulation is essential for pedestrian safety management and facility layout optimization. Data-driven models enhance trajectory prediction accuracy under Euclidean metrics, yet they suffer from excessively high collision rates, especially in bidirectional and multidirectional flows. In this paper, we establish a novel data-driven crowd simulation model that incorporates the pedestrian collision mechanism into the loss function to reduce collisions. A new lateral-acceleration-based collision loss function and a Voronoi-based motion feature extraction approach are proposed. The model is based on a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) architecture and is termed CPGAN (Collision-Penalized GAN). We evaluate CPGAN in bidirectional flow scenarios, which involve frequent collision avoidance behaviors. Results show that the proposed lateral-acceleration-based collision loss significantly reduces opposite-direction pedestrian collision rates to levels comparable with controlled experiments. CPGAN effectively simulates bidirectional flow, reproducing lane formation and N-t curves. The research outcomes can provide inspiration for integrating pedestrian dynamics mechanisms into loss functions in data-driven crowd simulation.

AI.tldr: CPGAN (Collision-Penalized GAN) is a data-driven crowd simulation model that incorporates a lateral-acceleration-based collision loss function and Voronoi-based motion feature extraction into a GAN architecture, significantly reducing collision rates in bidirectional and multidirectional flows while reproducing realistic lane formation and flow-density (N-t) curves.
AI.motivation: Existing data-driven crowd simulation models achieve high trajectory prediction accuracy under Euclidean metrics but suffer from excessively high collision rates, particularly in bidirectional and multidirectional flows, which limits their practical applicability for pedestrian safety management.
AI.method: The model introduces a novel lateral-acceleration-based collision loss function and a Voronoi-based motion feature extraction approach, integrated into a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) architecture, termed CPGAN. The collision mechanism is embedded directly into the loss function during training.
AI.result: CPGAN reduces opposite-direction pedestrian collision rates to levels comparable with controlled experiments, effectively simulates bidirectional flow, and successfully reproduces lane formation and N-t (flow-density) curves.
AI.conclusion: Integrating pedestrian dynamics mechanisms into loss functions is a promising direction for improving data-driven crowd simulation, and CPGAN demonstrates that collision-penalized learning can bridge the gap between data-driven accuracy and physics-based collision avoidance.

title: Diagnosing Failure Modes of Shared-State Collaboration in Resource-Constrained Visual Agents
summary: Modular visual reasoning systems increasingly rely on shared working memory for multi-step collaboration, yet the failure dynamics of intermediate state evolution in low-capacity regimes remain underexplored. We study failure modes of collaborative reasoning with weak learners (4B--8B models) through the lens of noise accumulation. We introduce CoSee, an auditing framework that formalizes the read-write-verify loop to trace information flow in document visual question answering. Across multi-page, chart, and web-based benchmarks, we find a counter-intuitive degradation: naive shared workspaces often amplify hallucinations rather than resolve them. We identify two dominant failure modes: Noise Reinforcement, where ungrounded notes are reused as evidence, and Policy Collapse, where added context shifts the model toward under-specified, short-form answers. Using cost-accuracy Pareto frontiers, we show that increased compute can correlate negatively with performance without explicit verification. Our findings suggest that for resource-constrained agents, the bottleneck lies not in reasoning depth but in communication fidelity, providing trace-level diagnostics and a mechanistic baseline for reliable modular design.

AI.tldr: CoSee reveals that shared working memory in modular visual reasoning systems with weak learners (4B-8B models) can amplify hallucinations rather than resolve them, identifying Noise Reinforcement and Policy Collapse as dominant failure modes, where increased compute may negatively correlate with performance without explicit verification.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to study failure dynamics of intermediate state evolution in low-capacity regimes for modular visual reasoning systems, particularly how shared working memory affects multi-step collaboration in weak learners (4B-8B models).
AI.method: The authors introduce CoSee, an auditing framework that formalizes a read-write-verify loop to trace information flow in document visual question answering. They evaluate across multi-page, chart, and web-based benchmarks using cost-accuracy Pareto frontiers.
AI.result: Naive shared workspaces amplify hallucinations rather than resolve them. Two dominant failure modes identified: Noise Reinforcement (ungrounded notes reused as evidence) and Policy Collapse (added context shifts models toward under-specified, short-form answers). Increased compute can correlate negatively with performance without explicit verification.
AI.conclusion: For resource-constrained agents, the bottleneck lies not in reasoning depth but in communication fidelity. The findings provide trace-level diagnostics and a mechanistic baseline for reliable modular design.

title: HARP-VLA: Human-Robot Aligned Representation Learning for Vision-Language-Action Model
summary: Learning generalizable vision-language-action (VLA) models from large-scale human videos is promising but challenging due to cross-embodiment discrepancies in both visual observations and executable actions. While latent action models reduce the action execution gap by learning action abstractions, they still rely on visual features. Thus, misaligned human and robot visual representations can lead to inconsistencies in policy inputs and induce domain-dependent latent actions, hindering effective co-training with human videos. To address this, we propose HARP, a human-robot aligned representation learning framework for more effective VLA pretraining from human videos. Specifically, HARP uses limited paired human-robot demonstrations as cross-embodiment bridges and abundant unpaired human and robot videos as a scalable dynamics supervision data source. It trains a robot-adapted visual encoder and a latent action model with manipulation-centric auxiliary cues and a source-relative pair-discriminative alignment loss, which adapts robot representations toward human semantics while preserving pair-level discrimination. The learned aligned vision encoder and latent action model provide a unified vision and action representation for VLA-style policy learning, where human and robot videos provide vision-language-to-latent-action supervision and a lightweight robot action head grounds latent actions into executable commands. Experiments on feature visualization, simulation, and realworld manipulation show improved human-robot alignment and downstream policy performance, achieving 4.481 average length on CALVIN ABC$\rightarrow$D and a 7.1\% realworld success rate gain over the strongest baseline.

AI.tldr: HARP is a human-robot aligned representation learning framework that uses limited paired demonstrations and abundant unpaired videos to train a robot-adapted visual encoder and latent action model, improving VLA pretraining from human videos and achieving 4.481 average length on CALVIN ABC→D and 7.1% real-world success rate gain.
AI.motivation: Learning generalizable VLA models from large-scale human videos is challenging due to cross-embodiment discrepancies in visual observations and executable actions. Misaligned human and robot visual representations cause inconsistencies in policy inputs and domain-dependent latent actions, hindering effective co-training with human videos.
AI.method: HARP uses limited paired human-robot demonstrations as cross-embodiment bridges and abundant unpaired human/robot videos as dynamics supervision. It trains a robot-adapted visual encoder and latent action model using manipulation-centric auxiliary cues and a source-relative pair-discriminative alignment loss, adapting robot representations toward human semantics while preserving pair-level discrimination.
AI.result: Achieves 4.481 average length on CALVIN ABC→D and a 7.1% real-world success rate gain over the strongest baseline, demonstrated through feature visualization, simulation, and real-world manipulation experiments.
AI.conclusion: The aligned vision encoder and latent action model provide unified vision and action representations for VLA-style policy learning, where human and robot videos provide vision-language-to-latent-action supervision, and a lightweight robot action head grounds latent actions into executable commands.

title: Learning to Adapt: Self-Improving Web Agent via Cognitive-Aware Exploration
comment: 24 pages
summary: Recent advances in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have led to promising progress in web agents. However, existing web agents often rely on handcrafted execution pipelines or expensive expert trajectories, limiting their adaptability to complex, dynamic environments. To address these challenges, we propose SCALE (Self-Cognitive-Aware Learning and Exploration), which leverages three adversarial roles, Selector, Predictor, and Judger to autonomously discover the agent's limitations and expand its cognitive boundaries through environmental exploration. Moreover, we propose SCALE-Hop, a graph exploration strategy that facilitates global planning and helps agents avoid local exploration traps. To further support learning, we construct SCALE-20k, a large-scale dataset collected from 19 real-world websites, containing diverse task types and structured demonstrations generated from SCALE's exploration traces. Experimental results show that our approach significantly improves the performance and generalization of multiple MLLMs in various web environments. Our framework offers a scalable and generalizable solution for building truly autonomous and adaptive web agents.

AI.tldr: SCALE introduces a self-cognitive-aware learning and exploration framework with three adversarial roles (Selector, Predictor, Judger) and a graph exploration strategy (SCALE-Hop) to improve MLLM-based web agents' adaptability, supported by a large-scale dataset SCALE-20k, achieving significant performance gains across diverse web environments.
AI.motivation: Existing web agents rely on handcrafted execution pipelines or expensive expert trajectories, limiting their adaptability to complex, dynamic environments.
AI.method: SCALE uses three adversarial roles (Selector, Predictor, Judger) to autonomously discover agent limitations and expand cognitive boundaries via environmental exploration, along with SCALE-Hop graph exploration strategy for global planning and avoiding local traps, and the SCALE-20k dataset derived from exploration traces.
AI.result: The approach significantly improves the performance and generalization of multiple MLLMs in various web environments.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers a scalable and generalizable solution for building truly autonomous and adaptive web agents.

title: Before Parc Fermé: RL-Time Pruning for Efficient Embodied LLMs in Autonomous Driving
summary:
Embodied Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used as reasoning modules in robotic control pipelines to improve human-robot interaction, but their memory and generation latency make real-time deployment difficult. Pruning can reduce these costs, but for controllers that undergo multiple pre- and post-training phases, the crucial question is not only how much to prune, but when pruning should occur.
  In this work, we propose Before Parc Fermé (BPF), a pruning strategy performed during RL that compresses embodied LLM controllers while they are still being optimized for closed-loop behavior. This allows pruning decisions to account for the task-specific supervision and closed-loop feedback that shape the final controller. We propose two variants: BPF-RL, which performs iterative pruning during RL by removing part of the model at predefined training intervals, and BPF-SFT/RL, which first prunes part of the model structure during SFT and then further compresses it during RL using the same iterative strategy as BPF-RL until the target pruning ratio is reached. We evaluate BPF on RobotxR1, an LLM-based autonomous-driving control pipeline, using an established LLM pruning framework (LLM-Pruner), and compare it against post-training pruning, post-training pruning with RL recovery, SFT-stage pruning, and smaller dense models from the same family.
  Our results show that BPF provides the best task-performance vs. memory and throughput trade-off among the considered pruning strategies. When compressing the larger RobotxR1 models, BPF-SFT/RL achieves a $1.69\times$ better size-end-to-end performance trade-off than directly selecting a smaller dense model from the same family, measured as removed parameters per lost percentage point of control adaptability. On the Jetson AGX Orin mounted on the target robotic platform, the compact models improve decode throughput by up to $27\%$.

AI.tldr: BPF is a pruning strategy performed during RL that compresses embodied LLM controllers while still being optimized for closed-loop behavior, achieving better task-performance vs. memory and throughput trade-offs than post-training pruning, with BPF-SFT/RL attaining 1.69× better size-performance trade-off and up to 27% throughput improvement on Jetson AGX Orin.
AI.motivation: Embodied LLMs used as reasoning modules in robotic control face high memory and generation latency hindering real-time deployment. Pruning can help but the timing of pruning (pre/post-training phases) is underexplored; existing approaches prune only after full training, missing opportunities to integrate task-specific supervision and closed-loop feedback into pruning decisions.
AI.method: Proposes Before Parc Fermé (BPF), a pruning strategy executed during RL training. Two variants: (1) BPF-RL — iterative pruning during RL at predefined intervals, (2) BPF-SFT/RL — first prunes during SFT then further compresses during RL with iterative pruning. Evaluated on RobotxR1 autonomous-driving LLM controller using LLM-Pruner framework.
AI.result: BPF achieves the best task-performance vs. memory and throughput trade-off among compared strategies. BPF-SFT/RL yields 1.69× better size-end-to-end performance trade-off than smaller dense models (measured as removed parameters per lost control adaptability percentage point). Compact models improve decode throughput by up to 27% on Jetson AGX Orin.
AI.conclusion: Pruning during RL (BPF) is superior to post-training pruning or SFT-only pruning for embodied LLM controllers. Jointly optimizing pruning decisions with closed-loop task feedback yields more efficient compressed controllers. BPF-SFT/RL outperforms even directly using a smaller dense model from the same family.

title: HypoAgent: An Agentic Framework for Interactive Abductive Hypothesis Generation over Knowledge Graphs
comment: Under Review
summary: Abductive reasoning over knowledge graphs aims to generate logical hypotheses that explain observed entities or facts. Existing controllable hypothesis generation methods allow users to guide this process with explicit conditions, but they remain limited in interactive settings: they struggle to ground evolving natural-language intents across multi-turn dialogues and provide little fine-grained diagnosis when generated hypotheses fail. To address these limitations, we propose HypoAgent, an Agentic framework for interactive abductive Hypothesis Generation over knowledge graphs. HypoAgent integrates three agents: an Intent Recognition Agent that grounds user utterances and dialogue history into executable KG conditions, a Hypothesis Generation Agent that performs controllable hypothesis generation according to the extracted user intention, and a Root Cause Analysis Agent that diagnoses unreliable hypothesis fragments and leverages KG neighborhood probing to identify supported refinements. Experiments on commonsense and biomedical domain-specific knowledge graphs demonstrate that HypoAgent achieves state-of-the-art semantic similarity under single-turn, multi-turn, and unconditional settings. Our code is available at https://github.com/HKUST-KnowComp/HypoAgent.

AI.tldr: HypoAgent is a multi-agent framework for interactive abductive hypothesis generation over knowledge graphs, integrating intent recognition, controllable hypothesis generation, and root cause analysis agents to handle multi-turn dialogues and diagnose failures.
AI.motivation: Existing controllable hypothesis generation methods struggle to ground evolving natural-language intents across multi-turn dialogues and provide little fine-grained diagnosis when generated hypotheses fail.
AI.method: HypoAgent integrates three agents: (1) an Intent Recognition Agent that grounds user utterances and dialogue history into executable KG conditions, (2) a Hypothesis Generation Agent that performs controllable hypothesis generation, and (3) a Root Cause Analysis Agent that diagnoses unreliable hypothesis fragments and leverages KG neighborhood probing for refinements.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art semantic similarity under single-turn, multi-turn, and unconditional settings on commonsense and biomedical domain-specific knowledge graphs.
AI.conclusion: The agentic framework effectively addresses interactive abductive reasoning limitations by grounding evolving intents and diagnosing hypothesis failures.

title: DeMaVLA: A Vision-Language-Action Foundation Model for Generalizable Deformable Manipulation
comment: 14 pages, 2 figures
summary: Real-world household robots require Vision-Language-Action (VLA) foundation models that can acquire reusable manipulation skills across diverse objects, task conditions, and household environments. Deformable-object folding is a representative challenge, requiring robots to handle clothing items from random initial states across varying categories, geometries, materials, and scenes. However, existing VLA systems commonly train separate policies for different object categories, while naively mixed multi-task training often suffers from task interference and degraded performance. To move beyond category-specific folding policies, we introduce DeMaVLA, a VLA foundation model for generalizable Deformable Manipulation. DeMaVLA adopts a VLM backbone with an action expert and formulates continuous action generation using flow matching. To improve efficiency, the action expert is constructed by pruning every other transformer layer while preserving layer-wise alignment with the VLM backbone, reducing training and inference cost. DeMaVLA is first pre-trained on approximately 5,000 hours of selected real-world dual-arm demonstrations to acquire general manipulation priors. It is then post-trained on mixed folding data that aggregates self-collected demonstrations and corrective trajectories from real-robot failures across multiple folding tasks through a human-in-the-loop Data Aggregation~(DAgger) pipeline. Experiments show that DeMaVLA achieves competitive performance on RoboTwin and strong real-world results on our household folding benchmark. These results highlight the value of scalable real-world data, efficient action generation, and corrective learning for general-purpose VLA policies in deformable-object manipulation.

AI.tldr: DeMaVLA is a VLA foundation model for generalizable deformable-object folding, using a VLM backbone with an efficient action expert (via layer pruning) and flow-matching-based action generation. It is pre-trained on ~5,000 hours of real-world dual-arm demonstrations and post-trained via human-in-the-loop DAgger with corrective data, achieving competitive performance on RoboTwin and strong real-world folding results.
AI.motivation: Existing VLA systems train separate policies for different object categories, and naively mixed multi-task training suffers from task interference and degraded performance. The goal is to move beyond category-specific folding policies to a single generalizable VLA foundation model for deformable manipulation across diverse objects, geometries, materials, and scenes.
AI.method: DeMaVLA uses a VLM backbone with an action expert for continuous action generation via flow matching. The action expert is constructed by pruning every other transformer layer while preserving layer-wise alignment with the VLM backbone to reduce cost. It is pre-trained on ~5,000 hours of real-world dual-arm demonstrations, then post-trained on mixed folding data via a human-in-the-loop DAgger pipeline that aggregates self-collected demonstrations and corrective trajectories from real-robot failures.
AI.result: DeMaVLA achieves competitive performance on RoboTwin and strong real-world results on the household folding benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Scalable real-world data, efficient action generation, and corrective learning are valuable for general-purpose VLA policies in deformable-object manipulation.

title: FAM-Bench: A Multimodal Benchmark for Condition-Aware Food-as-Medicine Reasoning
summary: Food-as-Medicine requires models to reason beyond what a dish is or what nutrition it contains: they must decide whether a concrete food choice is appropriate for a specific health condition. Existing food AI benchmarks primarily evaluate dish recognition, recipe understanding, nutrient estimation, or general nutrition question answering, leaving this health-aware decision layer largely untested. We introduce FAM-Bench, a multi-modal Food-as-Medicine benchmark with 2500 nutrition-expert-verified instances across 13 diet-related health conditions. The benchmark contains two complementary tasks: dish-level suitability assessment, where models judge whether a dish is suitable for a condition from its image and ingredient list, and comparative dish analysis, where models rank four candidate dishes by condition-specific suitability. Both tasks require integrating ingredient evidence, visual preparation cues, and clinical nutrition constraints, providing a standardized testbed for grounded health-aware reasoning in language and vision-language models.

AI.tldr: FAM-Bench is a multi-modal benchmark with 2500 expert-verified instances across 13 health conditions, testing whether AI models can judge dish suitability for specific medical conditions through dish-level assessment and comparative analysis tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing food AI benchmarks focus on dish recognition, recipe understanding, nutrient estimation, or general nutrition QA, but fail to test the critical health-aware decision layer where models must determine if a specific food choice is appropriate for a particular health condition.
AI.method: FAM-Bench contains 2500 nutrition-expert-verified instances across 13 diet-related health conditions, with two tasks: (1) dish-level suitability assessment (judging dish suitability from image + ingredient list) and (2) comparative dish analysis (ranking four candidate dishes by condition-specific suitability). Both tasks require integrating ingredient evidence, visual preparation cues, and clinical nutrition constraints.
AI.result: The benchmark provides a standardized testbed for evaluating grounded health-aware reasoning in language and vision-language models, revealing the gap between existing food AI capabilities and the clinical decision-making needed for Food-as-Medicine applications.
AI.conclusion: FAM-Bench fills a critical gap in food AI evaluation by introducing health-aware reasoning benchmarks, and serves as a standardized resource for advancing models toward clinically meaningful Food-as-Medicine applications.

title: AR Forcing: Towards Long-Horizon Robot Navigation World Model
summary: The diffusion based robot navigation world models are typically trained using parallel supervision, while autoregressive inference is employed during path planning. This results in a distribution shift between training and inference, which destabilizes the performance over long-horizon prediction. We propose AR Forcing, an autoregressive training strategy, which integrates the standard diffusion loss into the autoregressive training loop. At each step, the model uses its own predictions to update the context and optimize the single step noise prediction objective, thereby explicitly exposing the model to the inference state distribution during training. Our method does not require additional discriminators or distribution-matching losses, retains the original diffusion framework and sampler, and is easy to integrate. Experiments on multi-domain navigation datasets (RECON, SCAND, HuRoN, TartanDrive) show that compared with strong baselines, AR Forcing improved the consistency of generated images during long-horizon navigation and the accuracy of predicted trajectories, enhancing robustness of the model in complex known and unknown environments. We will release the code soon.

AI.tldr: Proposes AR Forcing, an autoregressive training strategy that integrates diffusion loss into autoregressive training loops to address distribution shift between parallel training and autoregressive inference in diffusion-based robot navigation world models, improving long-horizon prediction consistency and trajectory accuracy.
AI.motivation: Diffusion-based robot navigation world models suffer from distribution shift between parallel supervision training and autoregressive inference, causing instability in long-horizon predictions.
AI.method: AR Forcing integrates standard diffusion loss into the autoregressive training loop by using the model's own predictions to update context and optimize single-step noise prediction, explicitly exposing the model to inference-state distribution during training without additional discriminators or distribution-matching losses.
AI.result: On RECON, SCAND, HuRoN, and TartanDrive datasets, AR Forcing improved generated image consistency during long-horizon navigation and predicted trajectory accuracy over strong baselines, enhancing robustness in complex known and unknown environments.
AI.conclusion: AR Forcing effectively mitigates distribution shift in diffusion-based navigation world models, improving long-horizon prediction stability and trajectory accuracy while maintaining the original diffusion framework and sampler.

title: Answer-Set-Programming-based Abstractions for Reinforcement Learning
comment: Accepted for publication at the 42nd International Conference on Logic Programming (ICLP 2026). To appear in Theory and Practice of Logic Programming (TPLP)
summary: Reinforcement Learning (RL) enables autonomous agents to learn policies from experience, but realistic problems often involve enormous state spaces, making learning and generalisation challenging. Abstraction and approximation are therefore essential. Relational Reinforcement Learning (RRL) offers a way to reason about objects and their relations, and the CARCASS framework by Martijn van Otterlo demonstrates how logical representations can model Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) in first-order domains. Originally implemented in Prolog, CARCASS leverages domain knowledge to create powerful abstractions. We explore Answer-Set Programming (ASP), which is a rich and, contrary to Prolog, fully declarative modelling language, to realise CARCASS abstractions. We evaluate our ASP-based implementation in case studies of two domains, viz. Blocks World and Minigrid. Our results indicate that CARCASS with ASP provides a promising approach to constructing abstractions for RL, especially when domain knowledge is available.

AI.tldr: This paper explores using Answer-Set Programming (ASP) as a declarative alternative to Prolog for implementing CARCASS abstractions in Relational Reinforcement Learning, demonstrating promising results in Blocks World and Minigrid domains.
AI.motivation: Realistic RL problems involve enormous state spaces, making learning and generalization challenging; abstraction and approximation are essential. The CARCASS framework (originally in Prolog) offers logical abstractions for MDPs, but a fully declarative implementation could be beneficial.
AI.method: The authors replace Prolog with Answer-Set Programming (ASP), a fully declarative modelling language, to realize CARCASS abstractions for Relational Reinforcement Learning. They implement and evaluate this approach in two case study domains: Blocks World and Minigrid.
AI.result: The ASP-based implementation of CARCASS provides a promising approach for constructing abstractions in RL, particularly when domain knowledge is available, as demonstrated in both Blocks World and Minigrid domains.
AI.conclusion: CARCASS with ASP is a viable and promising approach for building relational abstractions in RL, especially when domain knowledge is available, offering advantages over the original Prolog-based implementation due to ASP's fully declarative nature.

title: Surface Constraint Policy for Learning Surface-Constrained and Dynamically Feasible Robot Skills
summary: Diffusion-based imitation learning methods have driven rapid progress in robot dexterous manipulation tasks. However, they have limitations when applied to tasks that involve complex free-form surface constraints because of their lack of explicit surface geometry constraint modeling and the dynamic feasibility issue, resulting in stochastic action generation that fails to achieve reliable surface alignment and maintain stable contact. To address these limitations, we propose a novel surface constraint policy (SCP) for generating robot actions that satisfy free-form surface constraints on the basis of human demonstrations and real-time visual observations. First, the surface geometry constraint is encoded using a two-dimensional weighted Gaussian kernel function that is derived from demonstrations. Building on the encoded surface geometry constraints, the diffusion-based policy is used to infer task-level action intentions from multimodal sensory inputs, including visual observations and robot state feedback. These intentions are further transformed into surface-constrained dynamic movement primitives (DMPs) through a similarity-based action mapping method, thereby enabling smooth and compliant motion execution. The SCP achieves generation of structured surface geometric intent and dynamically admissible actions. The proposed method is validated on multiple surface manipulation tasks and compared with existing techniques. The experimental results demonstrate superior task success rates and contact stability under surface constraints.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Surface Constraint Policy (SCP) that combines diffusion-based imitation learning with explicit free-form surface geometry modeling using Gaussian kernels and surface-constrained Dynamic Movement Primitives (DMPs), achieving superior task success rates and contact stability in dexterous manipulation tasks involving surface constraints.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion-based imitation learning methods lack explicit surface geometry constraint modeling and suffer from dynamic feasibility issues, leading to stochastic action generation that fails to achieve reliable surface alignment and stable contact in tasks involving complex free-form surface constraints.
AI.method: SCP first encodes surface geometry constraints using a 2D weighted Gaussian kernel function derived from demonstrations. A diffusion-based policy then infers task-level action intentions from multimodal sensory inputs (visual observations + robot state). These intentions are transformed into surface-constrained Dynamic Movement Primitives (DMPs) via a similarity-based action mapping method, enabling smooth and compliant motion execution.
AI.result: Validated on multiple surface manipulation tasks, the proposed method demonstrates superior task success rates and contact stability under surface constraints compared to existing techniques.
AI.conclusion: The SCP effectively generates structured surface geometric intent and dynamically admissible actions, overcoming the limitations of prior diffusion-based methods for surface-constrained manipulation tasks.

title: AutoSci: A Memory-Centric Agentic System for the Full Scientific Research Lifecycle
summary: Scientific research has traditionally been human-intensive, requiring researchers to coordinate literature, ideas, experiments, manuscripts, and review responses across long project cycles. The rise of LLM-based scientific agents creates an opportunity to automate this process. Such a system must support the full research lifecycle, maintain structured persistent memory across projects, and improve its own research procedures over time. However, existing systems either partially satisfy or fail to satisfy these requirements, leaving a gap for a unified automated scientific research system. As a result, we present AutoSci, a memory-centric agentic system for the full scientific research lifecycle. AutoSci is organized around four modules. SciMem provides schema-governed research memory, separating Long-Term Knowledge Memory for reusable scientific knowledge from Active Research Memory for project-level artifacts such as ideas, experiments, manuscripts, and reviews. SciFlow executes a five-stage lifecycle from literature understanding to rebuttal through a harness that controls state, context, verification, feedback, and orchestration. SciDAG augments difficult skills with DAG-shaped multi-agent operators and reusable stage-specific templates. SciEvolve converts feedback signals from users, experiments, reviews, and external environments into versioned updates to SciMem organization, SciFlow skills, and SciDAG templates. Together, these modules make AutoSci a persistent research environment that can execute, remember, and evolve across research projects. The code repository is available at https://github.com/skyllwt/AutoSci.

AI.tldr: AutoSci is a memory-centric agentic system that automates the full scientific research lifecycle using four modules: SciMem (structured research memory), SciFlow (five-stage execution lifecycle), SciDAG (DAG-shaped multi-agent operators), and SciEvolve (self-improvement via feedback).
AI.motivation: Scientific research is human-intensive and lacks unified automated systems that support the full research lifecycle, maintain persistent structured memory across projects, and improve their own procedures over time.
AI.method: AutoSci organizes around four modules: (1) SciMem—schema-governed memory separating Long-Term Knowledge Memory from Active Research Memory; (2) SciFlow—five-stage lifecycle (literature understanding to rebuttal) with harness-controlled state, context, verification, feedback, and orchestration; (3) SciDAG—DAG-shaped multi-agent operators with reusable templates for complex skills; (4) SciEvolve—converts feedback signals into versioned updates to memory, skills, and templates.
AI.result: AutoSci achieves a persistent research environment capable of executing, remembering, and evolving across research projects, addressing the gap in existing partial or insufficient systems.
AI.conclusion: AutoSci demonstrates a unified, memory-centric agentic architecture for full-lifecycle scientific research automation, with open-source code available for further development.

title: Learning Terrain-Aware Whole-Body Control for Perceptive Legged Loco-Manipulation
summary: Legged manipulators integrate exceptional terrain adaptability along with mobile manipulation capabilities, which make them highly promising for deployment in human-centric environments. By coordinating the control of both legs and arms, a whole-body controller can significantly expand the operational workspace of legged manipulators. However, many existing whole-body controllers primarily depend on proprioception and do not incorporate the critical exteroception required for effective terrain topology perception. This limitation can hinder their ability to adapt to varying environmental conditions and navigate complex terrains effectively. In this paper, we introduce TA-WBC, a terrain-aware whole-body control framework for legged manipulators, which features a novel RL-based unified policy tailored to whole-body loco-manipulation tasks in various terrains. Specifically, we employ a hybrid exteroception encoder to extract terrain features, providing an essential basis for the robot to proactively adapt posture and footholds. Furthermore, to facilitate stable cross-terrain loco-manipulation, we propose a novel end-effector sampling method based on the foot contact plane, decoupling manipulation target from base fluctuations. Moreover, a dual-policy distillation module is introduced to integrate expansive whole-body motion with terrain adaptability without catastrophic forgetting. The simulation and real-world experiments validate the robustness of our proposed controller, which leads to a larger reachable space, less tracking error, and reduced unexpected stumbles. This unified policy highlights the promising capabilities of legged manipulators in performing loco-manipulation tasks across complex terrains.

AI.tldr: TA-WBC is a terrain-aware whole-body control framework for legged manipulators using RL-based unified policy, hybrid exteroception encoder, end-effector sampling based on foot contact plane, and dual-policy distillation to achieve robust loco-manipulation across complex terrains with larger reachable space, less tracking error, and reduced stumbles.
AI.motivation: Existing whole-body controllers for legged manipulators rely primarily on proprioception and lack exteroception for terrain topology perception, limiting adaptability to varying environmental conditions and complex terrains.
AI.method: (1) Hybrid exteroception encoder to extract terrain features for proactive posture and foothold adaptation; (2) Novel end-effector sampling method based on foot contact plane to decouple manipulation from base fluctuations; (3) Dual-policy distillation module to integrate whole-body motion with terrain adaptability without catastrophic forgetting; (4) RL-based unified policy for whole-body loco-manipulation.
AI.result: Simulation and real-world experiments validate robustness, demonstrating larger reachable space, less tracking error, and reduced unexpected stumbles across complex terrains.
AI.conclusion: TA-WBC enables legged manipulators to perform loco-manipulation tasks across complex terrains with enhanced stability and workspace, highlighting their promise for deployment in human-centric environments.

title: LinTree: Improving LLM Reasoning with Explicitly Structured Search Histories
comment: 16 pages, 3 figures
summary: Large language models (LLMs) often solve reasoning problems by generating intermediate traces that explore and revise partial solutions. From a search perspective, these traces can be viewed as linearized search trees, where the model extends a partial solution, abandons it when it fails, and backtracks to try alternatives. Compared with traditional heuristic-guided search, such a policy has a potential advantage: it conditions on the whole search trace rather than only on the current local state. We first test whether LLMs utilize this advantage by comparing trace-conditioned reasoning policies against best-first search equipped with an LLM heuristic that only observes the current local state. Across three controlled reasoning environments, Blocks World, grid Navigation, and Sokoban, we find that raw access to search history alone is not enough to reliably outperform heuristic search. We then study one possible reason: in LLM reasoning traces, the underlying search tree is only implicitly represented, and when the model backtracks or switches branches, the trace does not explicitly identify which earlier search state is being revisited. We show that adding simple parent pointers to explicitly represent the linearized tree (LinTree) structure improves both task performance and search efficiency relative to implicit reasoning models and LLM-heuristic-guided search. These results suggest that search history becomes most useful when its tree structure is made explicit, motivating more structure-aware representations for LLM reasoning.

AI.tldr: LLMs solve reasoning problems by generating linearized search traces. Raw access to search history alone does not reliably outperform heuristic-guided search; however, making the underlying tree structure explicit (via parent pointers) improves both task performance and search efficiency over implicit reasoning and heuristic-guided approaches.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether LLMs benefit from conditioning on the entire search trace (beyond local state) during reasoning, and to determine if the implicit representation of search trees in LLM traces limits their effectiveness compared to traditional heuristic-guided search.
AI.method: Compared trace-conditioned LLM reasoning policies (which see full search history) against best-first search using an LLM heuristic (local state only) in three controlled environments: Blocks World, grid Navigation, and Sokoban. Then introduced LinTree, which adds explicit parent pointers to the linearized trace to represent tree structure, and compared its performance against both baselines.
AI.result: Raw search history alone does not reliably outperform heuristic-guided search. Adding explicit parent pointers (LinTree) improves both task performance and search efficiency relative to both implicit reasoning models and LLM-heuristic-guided search.
AI.conclusion: Search history becomes most useful when its underlying tree structure is made explicit, motivating structure-aware representations for LLM reasoning.

title: Haptic Sorter: A Unified Planning Framework for Online Shape Estimation and Real-Time Pose Inference
summary: Robotics manipulation usually assumes that the shape and pose of the object are known to the robot prior to motion planning. However, precise geometric information is not always available in practice, and pose inference suffers from sensor uncertainties and view occlusion. In this work, we propose a unified model-based geometric framework integrating robotic haptic perception, modeling, and manipulation planning. Our novelties involve: \textit{i)} Introducing Bayesian Optimization (BO) to guide the haptic exploration for object shape inference, where superellipses are used to approximate geometric boundary; \textit{ii)} Adaptive formulation of manipulation potential encoding object geometry for quasi-static robot-object interaction; \textit{iii)} Proposing an online Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE) for real-time pose inference based on model prediction and tactile feedback. We deploy our system on a 2D robotic sorting task, and vary object geometries to validate the robustness and generalizability of our framework in both simulation and a real-world multi-arm setup.

AI.tldr: A unified model-based geometric framework that integrates haptic perception, shape modeling (superellipses via Bayesian Optimization), adaptive manipulation potential, and online ODE-based pose inference for robotic manipulation without prior object knowledge, validated on 2D sorting tasks.
AI.motivation: Robotic manipulation typically requires known object shape and pose, but precise geometric information is unavailable in practice due to sensor uncertainties and occlusion.
AI.method: (i) Bayesian Optimization for haptic exploration guiding superellipse-based shape inference; (ii) adaptive manipulation potential encoding object geometry for quasi-static interaction; (iii) online ODE for real-time pose inference from model prediction and tactile feedback.
AI.result: Validated on a 2D robotic sorting task with varying object geometries in both simulation and real-world multi-arm setup, demonstrating robustness and generalizability.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework enables manipulation without prior geometric knowledge by integrating haptic exploration, shape modeling, and pose inference in a unified manner.

title: Choosing the Lens: Strategic Perspective Activation in Context-Dependent Argumentation
comment: Accepted to LAMAS&SR workshop at FLoC 2026
summary: The same arguments often need to be evaluated under different external regimes. An agent with influence over the regime has a strategic lever that standard formalisms do not directly capture. We introduce context-dependent argumentation frameworks (CDAFs), an extension of Dung's theory in which a defeat function determines, per context, which attacks succeed. A perspective-labeled specialisation derives the defeat function from a relevance set $ρ$ and a priority $π$. The relevance set is the agent's action space. In a small worked example, the agent's target argument is rejected under every full-relevance injective priority, yet accepted under partial activations, one of which no VAF audience can mirror. We define the corresponding decision problem, ACTIVATION-MANIPULATION, and record baseline complexity bounds. Tight bounds and multi-agent variants are left open.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Context-Dependent Argumentation Frameworks (CDAFs), an extension of Dung's theory where a defeat function determines attack success per context. A perspective-labeled specialization derives the defeat function from a relevance set and priority. The agent can manipulate argument acceptance by partially activating attacks, achieving outcomes no VAF audience can mirror. The ACTIVATION-MANIPULATION decision problem is defined with baseline complexity bounds.
AI.motivation: Standard argumentation formalisms do not capture the strategic lever of an agent who can influence which attacks succeed under different external regimes (contexts).
AI.method: CDAFs extend Dung's framework with a context-dependent defeat function. A perspective-labeled specialization derives this function from a relevance set ρ (agent's action space) and a priority π. The agent manipulates argument acceptance by partially activating attacks.
AI.result: The agent's target argument is rejected under every full-relevance injective priority but accepted under partial activations, one of which no VAF audience can replicate.
AI.conclusion: The ACTIVATION-MANIPULATION decision problem is defined with baseline complexity bounds; tight bounds and multi-agent variants remain open.

title: LiftNav: Path Planning via Semantic Lifting in TSDF-Guided Gaussian Splatting
summary: Autonomous robots in unknown indoor environments require both reliable collision avoidance and object-level understanding. Classical representations such as TSDF support safe planning but lack semantics, while photorealistic methods like Gaussian Splatting (GS) provide rich appearance yet suffer from soft geometry, limiting precise obstacle avoidance. We present LiftNav, a hybrid navigation framework built on GSFusion's TSDF+GS dual map, augmented with a real-time pipeline of YOLO-based detection, TSDF-based 3D lifting, and B-spline trajectory optimization. This design enables flexible semantic navigation without dense 3D embeddings. We further introduce a hinge-loss-based collision penalty that improves trajectory smoothness and safety. We evaluate our approach in a simulation using the Replica dataset. Compared against a state-of-the-art radiance field baseline we show a 100% feasibility rate and shorter trajectories.

AI.tldr: LiftNav is a hybrid navigation framework combining TSDF and Gaussian Splatting maps with YOLO detection, 3D lifting, and B-spline optimization to achieve semantic collision-free navigation in unknown indoor environments, achieving 100% feasibility and shorter paths than radiance field baselines.
AI.motivation: Autonomous robots in unknown indoor environments need both reliable collision avoidance (safety) and object-level understanding (semantics). Classical TSDF maps support planning but lack semantics; photorealistic GS offers rich appearance but has soft geometry, hindering precise obstacle avoidance.
AI.method: A hybrid framework built on GSFusion's TSDF+GS dual map, augmented with YOLO-based detection, TSDF-based 3D lifting, B-spline trajectory optimization, and a hinge-loss-based collision penalty for improved smoothness and safety.
AI.result: In simulation using the Replica dataset, LiftNav achieves 100% feasibility rate and shorter trajectories compared to a state-of-the-art radiance field baseline.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework effectively bridges the gap between geometric safety and semantic understanding for robot navigation, enabling flexible semantic navigation without dense 3D embeddings.

title: Adaptive Artificial Time-Delay Control with Barrier Lyapunov Constraints for Euler-Lagrange Robots
summary: This paper addresses the challenge of simultaneously compensating for state-dependent uncertainties and enforcing time-varying state constraints in Euler-Lagrange systems, a common requirement in robotics that remains underserved by existing control designs. A novel adaptive control framework is developed that combines an artificial time-delay-based uncertainty estimation strategy, also known as time-delay estimation, with a barrier Lyapunov function to enforce constraint-aware control design. Specifically, a state-dependent upper bound on the time-delay estimation approximation error is analytically formulated, and an adaptive law is constructed to estimate its parameters online, enabling real-time state-dependent uncertainty compensation without relying on prior model knowledge. To ensure constraint compliance, the barrier Lyapunov function-based controller enforces time-varying bounds on both position and velocity. The resulting architecture is provably stable via Lyapunov analysis. Experimental results on a five-degree-of-freedom robotic manipulator validate the framework's capability, compared with the state of the art, in maintaining strict adherence to safety-critical constraints under dynamic uncertainties.

AI.tldr: A novel adaptive control framework combining time-delay estimation with barrier Lyapunov functions to simultaneously compensate for state-dependent uncertainties and enforce time-varying position/velocity constraints in Euler-Lagrange systems, validated on a 5-DOF robot manipulator.
AI.motivation: Existing control designs for Euler-Lagrange systems (e.g., robotics) cannot adequately address the combined challenge of compensating for state-dependent uncertainties while enforcing time-varying state constraints, a critical requirement for safety-critical robotic applications.
AI.method: (1) An artificial time-delay estimation (TDE) strategy for uncertainty estimation; (2) A state-dependent upper bound on TDE approximation error analytically formulated with an adaptive law for online parameter estimation; (3) A barrier Lyapunov function (BLF)-based controller enforcing time-varying bounds on both position and velocity; (4) Lyapunov-based stability proof.
AI.result: Experimental validation on a five-degree-of-freedom robotic manipulator demonstrates strict adherence to safety-critical constraints under dynamic uncertainties, outperforming state-of-the-art approaches.
AI.conclusion: The proposed TDE-BLF adaptive control framework effectively achieves simultaneous uncertainty compensation and constraint enforcement without prior model knowledge, with provable stability and experimental validation on a real robot.

title: Shaft-integrated Force Sensing with Transformer-based Dynamics Compensation for Telesurgery
comment: The paper was accepted by IEEE Transactions on Medical Robotics and Bionics in May 2026
summary: Robot-Assisted Minimally Invasive Surgery (RAMIS) enhances surgeon dexterity, with newer platforms leveraging haptic feedback to further improve performance. Such force information has broader potential to inform performance assessment, tactile localization, and surgical autonomy. This motivates the need for accessible approaches to integrating force sensing into RAMIS tools. This work presents a method for integrating a six-axis commercial force sensor into the distal end of a standard cable-driven surgical instrument, enabling end-effector force measurement while preserving the original mechanical functionality of the device. The proposed design emphasizes reproducibility and accessibility for research applications, requiring no specialized manufacturing tools. A transformer neural network integrates force sensor measurements with robot state information to aid estimation of applied forces at the end-effector, compensating for internal cable forces arising from actuation. Our proposed approach achieved normalized errors below 6%, and generalized to unseen conditions better than purely proximal data-driven sensing approaches. High internal cable forces caused sensor saturation and reduced axial force observability, which can degrade performance along the tool's major axis and under higher load conditions. Given current levels of performance, the balance of system integrability and performance enables applications and research into timely topics of haptic feedback, skill assessment, and force-informed autonomy in RAMIS. Videos and code are available at https://enhanced-telerobotics.github.io/shaft force sensing.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a method to integrate a six-axis force sensor into the distal end of a cable-driven surgical instrument for RAMIS, using a transformer neural network to estimate end-effector forces. The approach achieves below 6% normalized error, generalizes better than proximal sensing, and enables research in haptic feedback, skill assessment, and autonomy.
AI.motivation: Force sensing in RAMIS has broader potential for performance assessment, tactile localization, and surgical autonomy, but accessible and reproducible integration approaches are lacking for standard cable-driven instruments.
AI.method: A six-axis commercial force sensor is integrated into the distal end of a cable-driven surgical instrument. A transformer neural network fuses sensor measurements with robot state information to estimate end-effector forces, compensating for internal cable forces from actuation. The design prioritizes reproducibility without specialized manufacturing.
AI.result: Normalized errors below 6%; better generalization to unseen conditions than purely proximal data-driven approaches; sensor saturation and reduced axial force observability under high cable forces degrade performance along the tool's major axis under higher loads.
AI.conclusion: The system achieves a practical balance of integrability and performance, enabling applications in haptic feedback, skill assessment, and force-informed autonomy in RAMIS.

title: Actuator-Aware Inverse Kinematics with Joint-Limit Admissibility for Torque-Controlled Redundant Robots
summary: This paper proposes actuator-aware inverse kinematics for torque-controlled redundant robots under joint-limit constraints. In the considered architecture, the inverse-kinematic output is not merely a purely kinematic joint-velocity command; it is the required joint velocity supplied to a downstream torque-level controller. Therefore, a small commanded task residual may not necessarily improve realized motion. The proposed method formulates a convex quadratic programming problem whose decision variable is the joint-level required velocity. Control barrier function style bounds impose reference-level joint-limit admissibility, while the task equation is handled through a penalized slack variable. Redundancy is resolved using a controller-compatibility objective that accounts for previous-command consistency and actuator torque-capacity weighting. The method is independent of the particular torque-level controller and can serve as an intermediate IK layer between an endpoint trajectory and a redundant robot controller. Experiments on a virtual-decomposition-controlled seven-degree-of-freedom upper-limb exoskeleton compare the method with standard inverse-kinematic baselines and a constrained task-preserving quadratic programming baseline. The results indicate lower limit-pushing commands, bounded admissible required velocities, and improved realized task behavior in the tested trajectory, without modifying the downstream controller.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an actuator-aware inverse kinematics method for torque-controlled redundant robots that formulates a convex quadratic programming problem with control barrier function bounds, controller-compatibility objectives, and slack variables to generate admissible joint velocity commands that improve realized task behavior under joint-limit constraints.
AI.motivation: Standard inverse kinematics outputs purely kinematic joint-velocity commands, which may not translate to good realized motion when passed to a downstream torque-level controller. A small kinematic task residual does not necessarily improve actual robot behavior.
AI.method: Formulates a convex quadratic programming problem where the decision variable is the required joint velocity. Uses control barrier function bounds for joint-limit admissibility, a penalized slack variable for the task equation, and a controller-compatibility objective balancing previous-command consistency and actuator torque-capacity weighting.
AI.result: Experiments on a 7-DOF upper-limb exoskeleton with virtual-decomposition control show lower limit-pushing commands, bounded admissible required velocities, and improved realized task behavior compared to standard IK baselines and a constrained task-preserving QP baseline, without modifying the downstream controller.
AI.conclusion: The method serves as an effective intermediate IK layer between endpoint trajectory and redundant robot controller, independent of the particular torque-level controller.

title: On-Device Robotic Planning: Eliminating Inference Redundancy for Efficient Decision-Making
comment: 19 pages
summary: Reasoning-based robotic policies using large language and vision-language models achieve strong semantic planning capabilities but mostly suffer from a high inference latency that limits practical real-time deployment. In this work, we observe that robotic reasoning workloads contain substantial temporal redundancy, where consecutive observations frequently produce identical actions and subgoals. Based on this insight, we present REIS, a human cognition inspired robotic decision-making framework that minimizes unnecessary reasoning while preserving semantic adaptability. REIS combines lightweight scene gating, KV-steered affordance routing, and deliberative reasoning to accelerate robotic control under embodied constraints. Experiments on ALFRED, and real-world robotic tasks demonstrate that REIS significantly suppresses reasoning overhead while maintaining competitive task performance.

AI.tldr: REIS is a robotic decision-making framework inspired by human cognition that reduces reasoning latency by exploiting temporal redundancy in consecutive observations, using scene gating, KV-steered affordance routing, and deliberative reasoning to accelerate control while maintaining task performance.
AI.motivation: Large reasoning-based robotic policies using LLMs/VLMs suffer from high inference latency that hinders real-time deployment. The authors identify that robotic reasoning workloads contain substantial temporal redundancy where consecutive observations often yield identical actions and subgoals.
AI.method: REIS combines three components: (1) lightweight scene gating to detect when reasoning is unnecessary, (2) KV-steered affordance routing to reuse cached reasoning, and (3) deliberative reasoning invoked only when needed — inspired by human cognition to minimize unnecessary computation.
AI.result: Experiments on ALFRED and real-world robotic tasks show that REIS significantly suppresses reasoning overhead while maintaining competitive task performance.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting temporal redundancy in robotic reasoning can dramatically reduce inference latency without sacrificing semantic planning capabilities, enabling practical real-time deployment of LLM/VLM-based robotic policies.

title: IDOL: Inverse-Dynamics-Guided Future Prediction for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
comment: 20 pages, 5 figures
summary: End-to-end autonomous driving has emerged as a compelling paradigm for learning planning directly from sensor observations, while recent world-model-based approaches further enrich this paradigm by enabling explicit reasoning about how the scene may evolve in the future. Yet future prediction alone does not guarantee better planning unless the predicted evolution can be converted into planning-relevant trajectory updates. Many current methods still forecast future scene states without explicitly decoding the motion implications hidden in state transitions. As a result, future reasoning often remains descriptively useful but only weakly coupled to executable motion generation. To address this limitation, we propose \mathbf{IDOL}, an inverse-dynamics-guided future prediction framework for world-model-based end-to-end planning in latent BEV space, where inverse dynamics serves as the key bridge between future prediction and trajectory optimization. IDOL first predicts multiple future latent scene states with a BEV world model, then applies an inverse dynamics model to adjacent latent futures to decode transition-aware trajectory features and recover planning-relevant motion deltas that explain how the latent world evolves over time. These inverse-dynamics-derived signals are used to optimize the planned trajectory, turning future forecasting from passive scene anticipation into actionable planning guidance. A lightweight closed-loop refinement module further improves long-horizon consistency by reusing the optimized trajectory for another round of future-aware reasoning. By introducing inverse dynamics into latent future reasoning, IDOL tightens the coupling between world modeling and planning. Extensive experiments on the NAVSIM v1 and NAVSIM v2 benchmarks show that IDOL achieves state-of-the-art performance among comparable methods.

AI.tldr: IDOL is an inverse-dynamics-guided future prediction framework for world-model-based end-to-end autonomous driving planning. It uses a BEV world model to predict future latent states, then applies inverse dynamics to decode motion deltas from adjacent latent frames, converting passive future forecasting into actionable planning signals. Experiments on NAVSIM benchmarks achieve state-of-the-art results.
AI.motivation: Existing world-model-based planning methods predict future scene states but struggle to tightly couple those predictions with executable trajectory generation, as future reasoning remains descriptively useful yet weakly connected to motion generation.
AI.method: IDOL (1) predicts multiple future latent scene states using a BEV world model; (2) applies an inverse dynamics model on adjacent latent futures to decode transition-aware trajectory features and recover planning-relevant motion deltas; (3) uses these motion deltas to optimize the planned trajectory; (4) includes a lightweight closed-loop refinement module for long-horizon consistency by reusing the optimized trajectory for another round of future-aware reasoning.
AI.result: State-of-the-art performance on NAVSIM v1 and NAVSIM v2 benchmarks among comparable methods.
AI.conclusion: Introducing inverse dynamics into latent future reasoning tightens the coupling between world modeling and planning, turning passive scene anticipation into actionable planning guidance.

title: Batched Differentiable Rigid Body Dynamics in PyTorch for GPU-Accelerated Robot Learning
summary: As robot control shifts toward large-scale reinforcement learning with in-loop dynamics computation, the community's reliance on CPU-bound libraries such as Pinocchio creates a throughput bottleneck in GPU-based training pipelines. We present BARD (Batched Articulated Rigid-body Dynamics), a self-contained PyTorch implementation of Featherstone's rigid-body dynamics algorithms, optimized for batched GPU evaluation and automatic differentiation. Three design choices make this efficient: a tiered lazy-evaluation cache that avoids redundant tree traversals, matmul-free joint transforms via pre-computed Rodrigues constants, and level-parallel propagation that reduces sequential operations to tree-depth batched steps. On five robot models (7-23 DOFs), BARD matches Pinocchio numerically while reaching up to 64x higher throughput for Forward Kinematics and 63x for Jacobians at batch size 4096 on an NVIDIA H200. We validate differentiability through gradient-based system identification on a 7-DOF manipulator, recovering link masses to 1.24% mean error under 5% torque noise, and integrate BARD into an Isaac Lab AMP training pipeline for an 11-DOF spined quadruped with 4096 parallel environments, where it is 8.5x faster than Pinocchio and 2.0x faster than ADAM for in-loop dynamics. BARD is open-sourced at: https://github.com/YueWang996/bard-pytorch-dynamics.

AI.tldr: BARD is a GPU-optimized, batched PyTorch implementation of Featherstone's rigid-body dynamics algorithms that achieves up to 64x higher throughput than Pinocchio for forward kinematics and 63x for Jacobians at batch size 4096, while supporting automatic differentiation. It uses three key design innovations: a tiered lazy-evaluation cache, matmul-free joint transforms via Rodrigues constants, and level-parallel propagation. Validated on five robot models (7-23 DOFs), it also demonstrates differentiable system identification and integrates into Isaac Lab AMP training with 8.5x speedup over Pinocchio.
AI.motivation: CPU-bound dynamics libraries like Pinocchio create a throughput bottleneck in GPU-based reinforcement learning pipelines that use in-loop dynamics computation, motivating the need for a batched, GPU-native dynamics solver.
AI.method: Three key design choices: (1) tiered lazy-evaluation cache avoiding redundant tree traversals, (2) matmul-free joint transforms via pre-computed Rodrigues constants, and (3) level-parallel propagation reducing sequential operations to tree-depth batched steps.
AI.result: Up to 64x higher throughput for Forward Kinematics and 63x for Jacobians at batch size 4096 vs Pinocchio on NVIDIA H200. Gradient-based system identification recovers link masses to 1.24% mean error under 5% torque noise. In Isaac Lab AMP training for 11-DOF spined quadruped with 4096 parallel environments, BARD is 8.5x faster than Pinocchio and 2.0x faster than ADAM.
AI.conclusion: BARD demonstrates that a GPU-native, batched, and differentiable rigid-body dynamics implementation can significantly outperform CPU-bound libraries in throughput, making it suitable for large-scale RL training with in-loop dynamics.

title: Learning Controlled Separation of Small Objects Between Two Fingers with a Tactile Skin
summary: We introduce and solve the novel task of controlled separation of small objects with two fingers of a multi-purpose robotic hand: after grasping into a box of small objects, the task is to drop as many of them until a desired number remains between the fingers. The objects are small compared to the width of the fingers but also in absolute terms. In our case little pellets with a diameter of only 6mm are handled. We show that the task can be performed purely tactile (no vision) using a spatially-resolved tactile skin on a fingertip. The separation policy is trained in simulation via reinforcement learning using a straightforward sparse reward, which basically checks if the desired number of objects is reached. In simulation experiments, we provide an exhaustive analysis of the benefits of using spatially-resolved tactile feedback: while an ideal (high-resolution) tactile sensor allows solving the task almost perfectly, a sensor with lower spatial resolution (here 4x4 taxels) still leads to an improvement of up to 20% compared to using only the fingers' joint sensors. For this analysis, we further train an estimator alongside the policy that predicts the ground truth contact positions. Finally, we demonstrate the successful sim-to-real transfer for the DLR-Hand II equipped with a tactile skin.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a novel task of controlled separation of small objects (6mm pellets) using two fingers of a robotic hand, solved purely through tactile feedback via reinforcement learning in simulation, with successful sim-to-real transfer on the DLR-Hand II. Spatially-resolved tactile sensing significantly improves performance over joint sensors alone, especially at higher resolutions.
AI.motivation: To enable a multi-purpose robotic hand to grasp a box of small objects and then release precisely a desired number of them between two fingers, using only tactile sensing (no vision), which is challenging due to the objects being much smaller than the fingers.
AI.method: The separation policy is trained via reinforcement learning with a sparse reward (checking if the desired object count is reached). The approach relies on a spatially-resolved tactile skin on the fingertip, and the analysis compares high-resolution tactile sensors, 4x4 taxel arrays, and joint-only sensors. A ground truth contact position estimator is also trained.
AI.result: Ideal high-resolution tactile sensing enables near-perfect task performance. A 4x4 taxel sensor yields up to 20% improvement over using only joint sensors. Successful sim-to-real transfer was demonstrated on the DLR-Hand II.
AI.conclusion: Spatially-resolved tactile feedback is crucial for controlled separation of small objects, and the proposed approach works in simulation and transfers effectively to a real robotic hand.
